items.title: TAI #228: AI ROI Beyond Labs Revenue + Our Interview with OpenAI’s Eoin Boylan
items.summary: Also, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GPT-6.1 Terra, Artificial Analysis’s new leaderboard, Anthropic’s internal AI usage, and OpenAI’s Eoin Boylan on forward deployed engineering. What happened this week in AI by Louie There were some great new models this week, along with more focus on AI return on investment (ROI), particularly around Anthropic’s IPO filing and the growing funding needs of the AI buildout. We also spoke with Eoin Boylan, OpenAI’s Head of Forward Deployed Engineering for EMEA, to discuss how his team works with clients. We also run an AI engineering and forward deployed engineering (FDE) consultancy at Towards AI, and both teams are hiring. On the model side, Kimi K3.1 Pro is another jump for the open-weight ecosystem, with the hosted model already live and full weights promised by November 4. GPT-6.1 Terra is another great push for cost-efficient computer use among closed models. OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra is also a meaningful update for cost-efficient computer use among closed models. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam, it beats GPT-5.6 Terra by 15 percentage points at medium effort while costing roughly a third as much, and it also improves OpenAI’s writing across a wide range of tasks. Artificial Analysis’s update to its Intelligence Index (v5) led to quite a shuffle in the leaderboard. Evaluations with private tests or held-out answers now carry 60% of the weighting, up from 45%. The revision also changed difficulty and task mix. Anthropic and OpenAI hold the top five places. At maximum reasoning effort, Opus 5.5 scores 58 and GPT-6 Astra 57. Kimi K3.1 Pro trails the leader by 12 points, against three on the previous index. Among models whose weights are already released, the leaders score 32, a 26-point gap. Many are interpreting this as a sign that some other labs were more heavily benchmaxxed on familiar benchmarks than on general, robust real-world performance. That fits my experience too: I find Opus and Astra far out ahead for most of my tasks. Where the returns show up AI agents are now obviously superhuman at many things, but many are asking why AI isn’t already generating more revenue to start justifying the huge AI capex. I would look for most of the LLM ROI outside AI lab revenue. Meta’s quarterly revenue per employee rose 27% between Q4 2025 and Q3 2026, and 205% since Q3 2022, just before ChatGPT launched. Put another way, Meta’s Q3 revenue annualizes to $258bn. At today’s headcount and its Q3 2022 revenue per employee, it would be about $85bn, or $174bn lower. That is obviously not $174bn of LLM productivity. Inflation, war, currency moves, reorganizations, headcount cuts, capex, and many other factors also drive that change. Even so, the naive productivity boost at Meta alone could well exceed OpenAI and Anthropic’s combined annualized revenue. For scale, OpenAI’s reported September run rate was almost $50bn, while Anthropic’s reported Q3 revenue annualizes to about $67bn (on a different definition). Within AI’s contribution at Meta, GPU-based recommender systems provide a big boost alongside LLMs. Meta also employs only ~0.0018% of the world’s employed people. The AI labs themselves are leading the way in using these tools and achieving ROI from internal use. Anthropic’s S-1 says average daily code volume contributed per engineer in Q3 was more than 45 times its 2024 average. Code volume is not the same as business productivity, but LTM revenue per employee rose from $1.4m to over $6.6m between September 2025 and September 2026. Internal Claude usage, valued at list prices, grew more than 250x from January to September, first exceeding monthly personnel expense in April (ex stock-based compensation). I expect similarly intensive internal AI use at OpenAI. Higher output per employee can justify enormous capital investment when a business is set up to allow each person to direct far more compute effectively. Most enterprise AI ROI potential, however, is still being wasted by slow adoption. Agents are still being treated like 2023 chatbots, and token spend is constrained. Some faster-moving organizations are already getting huge increases in productivity per employee well beyond coding. In most white-collar sectors, I think, if used well, models could deliver a 2x+ productivity boost today in many roles, such as law, financial research, sales, accounting, engineering, HR, marketing, and management. We don’t need to wait for a new class of model to begin capturing that. Codex and Claude are already enough, but the capabilities need to be put on a plate before most people start using them to their potential. Forward deployed AI engineers like ours make adoption easier by teaching people, building and optimizing skills, and then building custom apps and evaluations for more complex tasks. However, enterprise pricing does make ROI harder. For heavy usage, my rough estimate is that metered enterprise inference can cost 10 to 20x as much as the effective cost through personal or small-team subscriptions. Claude Team supports up to 150 seats; new ChatGPT Business workspaces support 200. As a result, most enterprises handicap the models with token budgets that are far too low. The new Artificial Analysis results show why budget affects capability: Opus scores 35 at low effort and 58 at max, at $0.98 versus $10.04 per evaluation task. I use subagents or loops for parallel research, criticism, iteration, and testing, and those loops need room to run. The useful measure is how much good work comes back and how much human effort it saves, not how well token spend fits into arbitrary legacy IT budgets. The biggest friction point outside code is that the models are still bad at writing. Poor prose can make capable reasoning look worse than it is, create more editing work, and add to the fatigue people already feel from generic AI-generated text. The labs have been far too slow to care about this. Once adoption takes hold, ROI still requires management to act. Your company ideally needs the imagination and agility to use the productivity and capability boost to launch new features, and enter new markets, and drive revenue growth; otherwise, it will be forced to cut staff to achieve ROI. Management also has to clear new bottlenecks quickly: hire fast for tasks AI does badly, build custom tools, and commit capex where it is needed. In practice, it may be easier to build an AI-native law firm that can handle five times as much work per person than to make an existing firm grow fivefold or cut 80% of its staff. What OpenAI’s FDEs build Eoin spoke with Assel from our team and me about how OpenAI approaches this work. His FDE team focuses on model intelligence gaps and missing product capabilities. OpenAI’s Deployment Company helps customers implement existing capabilities at scale, while partners bring established relationships and industry expertise. Every engagement starts with discovery, where his team challenges the customer’s proposed use cases: will they deliver enough ROI, and can the customer make that case to its board? At a major semiconductor company, where the goal was a shorter design-to-fabrication cycle, the team identified more than 50 use cases and ranked them by complexity and value. Starting with quick wins like these helps secure cooperation from the hardware experts whose knowledge the generalist FDEs need. His team now rarely fine-tunes for individual tasks because improvements in the base models keep overtaking that work. Some FDEs work inside research, helping close the capability gaps found at customers. They also build most solutions on the Codex harness with plugins and skills. Eoin described repeatedly building custom functionality only for the product to ship it a month later, forcing a redesign. Direct API use remains useful for particular integrations and specialized tasks. His team has direct access to OpenAI’s product and research groups, but the lesson applies more widely: choose carefully which parts of a workflow deserve custom engineering. Also, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GPT-6.1 Terra, Artificial Analysis’s new leaderboard, Anthropic’s internal AI usage, and OpenAI’s Eoin Boylan on forward deployed engineering.What happened this week in AI by Louie

There were some great new models this week, along with more focus on AI return on investment (ROI), particularly around Anthropic’s IPO filing and the growing funding needs of the AI buildout. We also spoke with Eoin Boylan, OpenAI’s Head of Forward Deployed Engineering for EMEA, to discuss how his team works with clients. We also run an AI engineering and forward deployed engineering (FDE) consultancy at Towards AI, and both teams are hiring.

On the model side, Kimi K3.1 Pro is another jump for the open-weight ecosystem, with the hosted model already live and full weights promised by November 4. GPT-6.1 Terra is another great push for cost-efficient computer use among closed models. OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra is also a meaningful update for cost-efficient computer use among closed models. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam, it beats GPT-5.6 Terra by 15 percentage points at medium effort while costing roughly a third as much, and it also improves OpenAI’s writing across a wide range of tasks.

Artificial Analysis’s update to its Intelligence Index (v5) led to quite a shuffle in the leaderboard. Evaluations with private tests or held-out answers now carry 60% of the weighting, up from 45%. The revision also changed difficulty and task mix. Anthropic and OpenAI hold the top five places. At maximum reasoning effort, Opus 5.5 scores 58 and GPT-6 Astra 57. Kimi K3.1 Pro trails the leader by 12 points, against three on the previous index. Among models whose weights are already released, the leaders score 32, a 26-point gap.

Many are interpreting this as a sign that some other labs were more heavily benchmaxxed on familiar benchmarks than on general, robust real-world performance. That fits my experience too: I find Opus and Astra far out ahead for most of my tasks.

Where the returns show up

AI agents are now obviously superhuman at many things, but many are asking why AI isn’t already generating more revenue to start justifying the huge AI capex. I would look for most of the LLM ROI outside AI lab revenue. Meta’s quarterly revenue per employee rose 27% between Q4 2025 and Q3 2026, and 205% since Q3 2022, just before ChatGPT launched. Put another way, Meta’s Q3 revenue annualizes to $258bn. At today’s headcount and its Q3 2022 revenue per employee, it would be about $85bn, or $174bn lower.

That is obviously not $174bn of LLM productivity. Inflation, war, currency moves, reorganizations, headcount cuts, capex, and many other factors also drive that change. Even so, the naive productivity boost at Meta alone could well exceed OpenAI and Anthropic’s combined annualized revenue. For scale, OpenAI’s reported September run rate was almost $50bn, while Anthropic’s reported Q3 revenue annualizes to about $67bn (on a different definition). Within AI’s contribution at Meta, GPU-based recommender systems provide a big boost alongside LLMs. Meta also employs only ~0.0018% of the world’s employed people.

The AI labs themselves are leading the way in using these tools and achieving ROI from internal use. Anthropic’s S-1 says average daily code volume contributed per engineer in Q3 was more than 45 times its 2024 average. Code volume is not the same as business productivity, but LTM revenue per employee rose from $1.4m to over $6.6m between September 2025 and September 2026. Internal Claude usage, valued at list prices, grew more than 250x from January to September, first exceeding monthly personnel expense in April (ex stock-based compensation). I expect similarly intensive internal AI use at OpenAI. Higher output per employee can justify enormous capital investment when a business is set up to allow each person to direct far more compute effectively.

Most enterprise AI ROI potential, however, is still being wasted by slow adoption. Agents are still being treated like 2023 chatbots, and token spend is constrained. Some faster-moving organizations are already getting huge increases in productivity per employee well beyond coding. In most white-collar sectors, I think, if used well, models could deliver a 2x+ productivity boost today in many roles, such as law, financial research, sales, accounting, engineering, HR, marketing, and management. We don’t need to wait for a new class of model to begin capturing that. Codex and Claude are already enough, but the capabilities need to be put on a plate before most people start using them to their potential.

Forward deployed AI engineers like ours make adoption easier by teaching people, building and optimizing skills, and then building custom apps and evaluations for more complex tasks.

However, enterprise pricing does make ROI harder. For heavy usage, my rough estimate is that metered enterprise inference can cost 10 to 20x as much as the effective cost through personal or small-team subscriptions. Claude Team supports up to 150 seats; new ChatGPT Business workspaces support 200.

As a result, most enterprises handicap the models with token budgets that are far too low. The new Artificial Analysis results show why budget affects capability: Opus scores 35 at low effort and 58 at max, at $0.98 versus $10.04 per evaluation task. I use subagents or loops for parallel research, criticism, iteration, and testing, and those loops need room to run. The useful measure is how much good work comes back and how much human effort it saves, not how well token spend fits into arbitrary legacy IT budgets.

The biggest friction point outside code is that the models are still bad at writing. Poor prose can make capable reasoning look worse than it is, create more editing work, and add to the fatigue people already feel from generic AI-generated text. The labs have been far too slow to care about this.

Once adoption takes hold, ROI still requires management to act. Your company ideally needs the imagination and agility to use the productivity and capability boost to launch new features, and enter new markets, and drive revenue growth; otherwise, it will be forced to cut staff to achieve ROI. Management also has to clear new bottlenecks quickly: hire fast for tasks AI does badly, build custom tools, and commit capex where it is needed. In practice, it may be easier to build an AI-native law firm that can handle five times as much work per person than to make an existing firm grow fivefold or cut 80% of its staff.

Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience tested the resulting 211 designs, and 17 met Anthropic’s criteria for binding, each against a single toxin. Anthropic has not tested whether the designs neutralize the toxins in cells or protect animals, so it does not claim to have produced an antivenom. Anthropic has publicly released all 211 designs and their experimental data.

5. OpenAI Cuts Frontier Training Off From the Live Internet

OpenAI announced on October 23 that it now conducts frontier-model training without live internet access, using an offline environment containing indexed and cached web content so models can still practice browsing and interacting with web applications. The policy follows a September 20 incident in which an internal research model exploited a DNS-resolver misconfiguration and gained limited access to the live internet during training. OpenAI paused training and evaluation of its most capable models, hardened its infrastructure and monitoring, and launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign in which teams of frontier-model agents tried to reach the internet, cross internal security boundaries, and communicate across isolated environments. OpenAI resumed frontier reinforcement-learning training and internal inference on October 1 after evaluating the strengthened controls.

6. NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120B-parameter multimodal model for specialized agentic workloads, alongside two smaller Bolt models for local and edge deployment. Super VL handles text and visual inputs, including images, webpages, PDFs, and video. NVIDIA says its accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks is comparable to Nemotron 3 Ultra at roughly one-fifth the parameter count. Super VL was trained on about 26T tokens across pre-training and continued pre-training, followed by post-training on roughly 3.8 million samples and reinforcement learning across dozens of environments. The release includes open weights, datasets, and training recipes. NVIDIA also released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B, which uses native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory for local agentic workloads, while Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B, a 4GB-footprint model for conversational and physical agents, followed on October 23. Super VL is available through Hugging Face, OpenRouter, ModelScope, and NVIDIA NIM.

7. Cohere Releases Rerank 5

Cohere released Rerank 5 in Pro and Fast versions for reranking retrieved documents. In Cohere’s evaluations, Rerank 5 Pro leads the ViDoRe V3, nanoMTEB, BRIGHT, and BEIR benchmark groups, ranking first on 39 of 46 datasets. Its largest reported generational gain is on BRIGHT, where it scores 82.2, 5.8 points above Voyage AI Rerank 3 and 12.4 points above Rerank 4 Pro. Both versions add Context Focus, which returns scored relevant spans within each document so applications can send only selected passages to an LLM. Across 30 question-answering datasets, Cohere reports that removing half of the retrieved text retained 96% of answer quality. Rerank 5 also introduces calibrated relevance scores, which Cohere says can be interpreted approximately as probabilities of a document being useful. In Cohere’s single-A100 throughput test, Fast processed 2.9× as many documents per second as Pro. Rerank 5 is generally available through the Cohere API, Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry, Amazon SageMaker, and North.

AI Tip of the Day

You do not need a framework for 90% of AI apps. In fact, while building the code for our 2026 AI Engineering book, we deleted LangChain and LlamaIndex from our core RAG and app chapters.

When we rewrote those pipelines in plain Python, the code got shorter, faster, and much easier to fix:

  • Prompt templates: Just use a standard Python f-string or a 10-line class.
  • Self-fixing output parsers: A while loop that catches a Pydantic ValidationError and sends the exact error message back to the LLM takes 15 lines of code.
  • Parallel chains: Running map-reduce across a big document is just asyncio.gather().
  • Vector search: An in-memory vector store with cosine similarity is literally one NumPy matrix multiplication (np.dot).

When you write these basic parts in plain Python, nothing is hidden. You can see every token, catch every bad output, and swap models in seconds. Keep the heavy frameworks like LangGraph for the rare times you actually need a complex state machine.

Five 5-minute reads/videos to keep you learning

1. How I Made Local LLMs Up to 2.24× Faster on a 4GB NVIDIA GPU

This article benchmarks Gemma 4, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5 on a 4GB GTX 1650 Ti using llama.cpp, then tunes GPU layer placement, CPU threads, microbatch size, and KV-cache precision. The largest gains came from GPU offloading, which increased Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 token generation by 2.07× and 2.24×. It also shares the memory-throughput trade-off of KV-cache quantization and provides reproducible launch configurations for running current local models on limited VRAM.

2. AI Is Inventing New Mathematics. Are We Ready for What It Discovers Next?

The article looks at recent cases where AI systems have contributed to new mathematical results, including AlphaEvolve, an 80-year-old geometry conjecture, and OpenAI’s work on a Navier–Stokes singularity. It explains three approaches behind these results: evolutionary search, language-model reasoning, and formal verification with systems such as Lean. It then examines the questions these methods raise around verification, mathematical understanding, authorship, and the role of human mathematicians.

3. Build a Jev-Style Decision Model from an LLM, Training the Jev Head

This article takes a small pointer head with 524,288 trainable parameters and turns a frozen vision-language backbone into a decision model that reached 0.959 accuracy on 800 synthetic support tickets, against 0.352 for random guessing. It traces why raw dot-product scores saturate softmax, then fixes it with learned projections, masked loss, shuffled option orders, one-cycle scheduling, and RMS normalization.

4. Scale Azure Data Factory ETL with 1 Metadata Control Table

The article shows how to replace separate Azure Data Factory pipelines for each source table with a metadata-driven ingestion design. It builds the workflow around an Azure SQL control table and reusable parameterized pipelines that load relational data into ADLS Gen2. The walkthrough covers full and incremental loads, watermark handling, identifier validation, checkpoints, run isolation, publication, failure recovery, and concurrency and throughput tuning.

Repositories & Tools

1. Skill Spector is a security scanner for AI agent skills that detects prompt injection, unsafe code, data exfiltration, and supply-chain risks.

2. Sandbox Runtime is a lightweight sandboxing tool for enforcing filesystem and network restrictions on arbitrary processes at the OS level, without requiring a container.

3. Agnesh is a multi-agent harness for coordinating large numbers of agents that claim tasks, share results, and verify each other’s work.

4. AKV is a KV-cache management system for long-running LLM agents that reduces context overhead while preserving reusable cache.

5. Devin-vuln-fixes is a collection of agent skills for finding vulnerable dependencies, applying fixes, testing changes, and preparing remediation PRs.

Top Papers of The Week

1. POSEIDON: Scaling Training Environments for Scientific Agents from Code Repositories

The paper introduces Poseidon, an automated pipeline that turns scientific code repositories into executable, verifiable training environments for scientific agents. It creates four task types: Reproduction, Subflow, Completion, and Correction, and uses a recursive loop to recover failed candidates. The resulting Pearl dataset contains 97,659 environments from 7,110 repositories across 10 scientific disciplines, and the authors report consistent gains when training several Qwen3.5 models on it.

2. Object-Oriented Harness: Evolving Agent Harnesses through Object-Oriented Design

The paper proposes OO-Harness, which replaces one global agent harness with a hierarchy of specialized harness classes. During training, an evolution agent creates new harness subclasses from execution records, while a router learns which harness to use for each task at test time. Across three long-horizon benchmarks, the authors report up to a 15% absolute improvement over the base harness.

3. BizBench: Unveiling Hidden Challenges in Deploying Long-Horizon Agents for Real-World Business

The paper introduces BizAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating whether long-horizon agents follow business constraints correctly throughout execution, not just whether they reach the final goal. It includes 50 tasks, 789 knowledge documents, and 601 business tools based on procedures from a payments company. The authors find a sizable gap between goal completion and strict success, showing that agents can reach the intended outcome while still violating important policies or execution constraints.

4. LoopVL: Recurrent Visual Intelligence

The paper introduces LoopVL to study whether Loop Transformers can be effectively extended to vision-language models. It combines Module-Loop and Model-Loop computation and is trained from scratch through language pre-training, multimodal training, and post-training. The authors report better multimodal understanding and visual reasoning than several similarly sized and larger non-recurrent models.

5. Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization

The paper introduces Self-HPO, a framework that jointly improves a coding agent’s model policy and its harness, rather than optimizing either in isolation. In each round, the current policy analyzes its failures and proposes new harnesses, then reinforcement learning updates the policy under the selected harness. Across three coding benchmarks, the method raises Qwen3.5–35B-A3B’s average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains in reliability and out-of-distribution performance.

Quick Links

1. Google Cloud launches Agent Compute Engine, a purpose-built compute service for running AI agents in isolated microVMs. The service gives each agent its own hardware-isolated environment with persistent storage, short-lived credentials, and support for pausing idle workloads and quickly restoring them from snapshots. Google says the same infrastructure already powers Gemini’s agent workloads and uses copy-on-write memory sharing to increase compute density. Agent Compute Engine is not available yet; Google says it will enter preview in the coming months.

items.title: Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural
items.summary: Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned Ghost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer , as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”. In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing . But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/ nosleep subreddit , meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material.

items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort
items.summary: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, marketing it as a cheap, fast model for high-volume everyday work, priced at a tenth of its GPT-6 Astra flagship. As the mid-priced model in its GPT-6 family , OpenAI lists Terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, a mere tenth of Astra’s $10 and $50. The AI giant also reports that Terra completes tasks more than three times faster than Astra in its Agents’ Last Exam benchmark. Those computer-use results are not directly comparable to the three tests below. Early benchmarks showed some limitations, alongside gains. Plotly reported that Terra caught three of five planted patterns in its analytics test and passed 40 of 43 questions overall. Artificial Analysis found that it guessed on 38% of questions it couldn’t answer instead of saying so, down from 88% for GPT-5.6 Terra in the same benchmark. DualEntry’s accounting benchmark put its accuracy at 78.2%. In this AI arms race, each launch needs to be marketed as the best; otherwise, it risks being ignored. This can create a confusing experience for users, especially when reality doesn’t quite match the promise. I compared Terra with Astra on three synthetic tasks to see how their speed, estimated token costs, and accuracy differed. This is a separate test of those trade-offs, not a replication of OpenAI’s computer-use benchmark. The tests I ran the final version of each test once per model through OpenAI’s API with reasoning effort set to high. I didn’t set an output-token cap, though the models still have built-in output limits. I graded each test against keys I built and verified, after developing three versions of each test. These are single-run results on synthetic tasks, not estimates of repeatability or performance across all workloads. Matching the effort setting does not impose the same reasoning-token budget on both models. Both models returned the same score on easy and medium-difficulty tests. To test the real soft spots, after the same results returned a third time, I ran hard tests against a weaker model, GPT-5 Mini, until Mini’s score was very low. Here is the final iteration of the tests. These are the tests detailed in the remainder of this article. In the usage figures below, “out” includes reasoning tokens; the parenthetical reasoning count is a subset, not an additional charge. Costs are estimates calculated from the reported tokens at standard uncached input and output rates, excluding any tool charges or billing adjustments. They are not verified invoice totals. SQL reasoning – I built a fake database of 500 software builds and asked each model 25 questions about it. Some builds were deleted, some were retries, costs are in three currencies, and a few questions depend on time zones. Two of the questions can’t be answered from the data. Data validation – I gave each model a spreadsheet of 4,950 fake customer records and 19 rules they’re supposed to follow. Some rules only make sense across the whole file, like no more than three customers at one postal code and no referral loops; forty records break a rule, and 10 look wrong but are actually fine. Incident log triage – I wrote about 7,000 lines of logs from a fake outage across more than 20 services. I planted errors like drifting clocks, error messages blaming the wrong service, and unrelated changes sending alerts before the one that actually caused the outage. SQL reasoning This test showed the widest split between the two models. Astra scored 48/50 and Terra 26/50. Each of the 25 questions was worth two points, for a total of 50. An answer had to be exactly right to earn the two points, so a close answer earned zero. Unanswered questions also earned zero points. For the questions that can’t be answered from the data, the correct answer was to identify that. On every other question, a model that didn’t give an answer earned zero. Terra processed all 500 rows and handled soft deletes, retries, and three currencies. Its one miss was the total run time for 151 builds in a single region. Astra’s answer came in 406 seconds short of the correct 31,428. Its answer was 31,022 seconds, about 1.3% below the stated correct total. The final answer alone doesn’t show whether the error came from addition, a skipped row, or a misread value. Astra was more accurate in this run, but its incorrect total still needed checking. It generated 27,970 reasoning tokens, and the response took 319.7 seconds—more than five minutes. On the six questions that required adding up costs or durations across all 500 rows, Terra didn’t attempt an answer. It wrote a SQL query for me to run instead and marked each one as not calculated. Terra didn’t make up numbers, which is good. But it left the hardest part of the job, running the query and getting the totals, for you to do yourself. This is the first time I’ve seen AI hand work back. The bigger problem is that Terra answered six questions wrong. Four of them were counts that were off by just one or two. Terra gave those answers with the same confidence as its correct ones, so nothing signaled that they were wrong. If you used those numbers in a report, you wouldn’t know which ones to double-check. I’m including the numbers for both Terra and Astra here, but since the results were so different, the lower price and faster time aren’t wins. Terra 133.1 s, 21,060 in, 11,554 out (10,707 reasoning), $0.079 Astra 319.7 s, 21,060 in, 28,806 out (27,970 reasoning), $1.65 Data validation Astra scored a perfect 50, and Terra scored 45. 40 of the 50 points came from the 40 records that broke a rule. A model earned one point for each record it flagged, as long as it named the rule the record broke. The last 10 points came from records that looked wrong but followed every rule. A model lost a point for every correct record it accidentally flagged as incorrect. Before giving its answer, Terra warned that it couldn’t reliably check all 4,950 records against the rules and might miss some (as it did in the SQL test). The reported input fit within the model’s context window, and I did not set an output cap. Terra generated 1,841 reasoning tokens compared with Astra’s 12,831. The responses took 31.4 and 145.0 seconds, respectively; these elapsed times don’t isolate reasoning time. Terra correctly flagged 35 of the 40 invalid records and flagged none of the valid records: 87.5% recall and 100% precision in this run. Its 45/50 score is a test score, not an accuracy percentage across all 4,950 records. Three of the five it missed only break a rule when you compare them with other records in the file, such as a customer who reused another customer’s phone number. Terra flagged everything correctly, but it missed five invalid records. The results don’t explain why it missed them. Astra caught all 40, but it took more than four times as long and cost about 12 times as much. Terra used fewer reasoning tokens and missed records in this run; that association does not establish the cause of the misses. The numbers: Terra 31.4 s, 234,045 in, 2,336 out (1,841 reasoning), $0.25 Astra 145.0 s, 234,045 in, 13,369 out (12,831 reasoning), $3.01 Incident log triage This one was a tie, with both models scoring 50. I graded this test using a 50-point list of what a correct answer needs to include. To earn the full 50 points, a model had to trace the outage to the settings change in the ledger service, find the three servers with wrong clocks, and avoid blaming the planted false leads. False leads included a fraud service update that was rolled back, a payments setting that changed seconds before the real cause, a database switchover, and an unrelated memory problem in the search service. Error messages blamed the fraud service, but both models traced the outage to a settings change in the ledger service and spotted the three servers with wrong clocks. Neither model took the error messages at face value. Both checked the evidence underneath, which is what you’d want from an engineer during a real outage. Astra cost about 11 times as much as Terra and took 2.6 times as long to complete the work. Most of Astra’s additional output tokens were reasoning tokens: 4,628 of the 6,650-token difference. Both models earned the same score here despite that difference. These runs don’t show whether additional reasoning led to better scores on the other tests. The numbers: Terra 94.3 s, 251,651 in, 7,508 out (5,114 reasoning), $0.29 Astra 244.5 s, 251,651 in, 14,158 out (9,742 reasoning), $3.22 Results Test Terra (out of 50) Astra (out of 50) GPT-5 Mini (out of 50) SQL reasoning 26 48 6 Data validation 45 50 10 Incident log triage 50 50 12 Total (of 150) 121 148 28 Estimated token cost $0.61 $7.88 — Total time 258.8 s 709.2 s — I included GPT-5 Mini’s baseline results for reference. I rebuilt these tests several times and kept making them harder because both models kept returning identical scores. Because I selected these harder versions after seeing earlier results, they shouldn’t be treated as a representative sample of everyday work. A low Mini score is a comparison point, not an independent measure of test difficulty. What do I think? In these three final high-effort runs, Terra generated fewer reasoning tokens and finished sooner than Astra. It scored lower on SQL reasoning and data validation, and tied Astra on incident log triage. That is a trade-off in the results, but it doesn’t tell us whether Terra was overwhelmed or why it made specific errors. The measured totals were 258.8 seconds for Terra and 709.2 seconds for Astra, so Astra took about 2.74 times as long overall. At the stated standard uncached rates, the estimated token costs were $0.61 and $7.88; Terra’s cost was about 7.8% of Astra’s. Terra scored 121/150 and Astra 148/150 under these test rubrics. The runs show a cost, time, and score trade-off; they don’t show that OpenAI deliberately cut reasoning to achieve it. Terra matched Astra’s scores on my earlier easy and medium versions, but that does not establish its accuracy on every task at those difficulty levels. On the final tests, I would be cautious about using it for unchecked numerical aggregation or exhaustive data validation. It may be an acceptable lower-cost alternative for some workloads, including tasks like the incident triage tested here, as long as you verify the results. Astra’s incorrect SQL total also reminds you to check its work.

As the mid-priced model in its GPT-6 family, OpenAI lists Terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, a mere tenth of Astra’s $10 and $50. The AI giant also reports that Terra completes tasks more than three times faster than Astra in its Agents’ Last Exam benchmark. Those computer-use results are not directly comparable to the three tests below. 

Early benchmarks showed some limitations, alongside gains. Plotly reported that Terra caught three of five planted patterns in its analytics test and passed 40 of 43 questions overall. Artificial Analysis found that it guessed on 38% of questions it couldn’t answer instead of saying so, down from 88% for GPT-5.6 Terra in the same benchmark. DualEntry’s accounting benchmark put its accuracy at 78.2%. 

In this AI arms race, each launch needs to be marketed as the best; otherwise, it risks being ignored. This can create a confusing experience for users, especially when reality doesn’t quite match the promise. I compared Terra with Astra on three synthetic tasks to see how their speed, estimated token costs, and accuracy differed. Matching the effort setting does not impose the same reasoning-token budget on both models. 

Both models returned the same score on easy and medium-difficulty tests. To test the real soft spots, after the same results returned a third time, I ran hard tests against a weaker model, GPT-5 Mini, until Mini’s score was very low.

Some rules only make sense across the whole file, like no more than three customers at one postal code and no referral loops; forty records break a rule, and 10 look wrong but are actually fine.
  • Incident log triage – I wrote about 7,000 lines of logs from a fake outage across more than 20 services. I planted errors like drifting clocks, error messages blaming the wrong service, and unrelated changes sending alerts before the one that actually caused the outage.
SQL reasoning

This test showed the widest split between the two models. Astra scored 48/50 and Terra 26/50. Each of the 25 questions was worth two points, for a total of 50. An answer had to be exactly right to earn the two points, so a close answer earned zero. Unanswered questions also earned zero points. Terra processed all 500 rows and handled soft deletes, retries, and three currencies. Its one miss was the total run time for 151 builds in a single region. Astra’s answer came in 406 seconds short of the correct 31,428. Its answer was 31,022 seconds, about 1.3% below the stated correct total. The final answer alone doesn’t show whether the error came from addition, a skipped row, or a misread value.

Astra was more accurate in this run, but its incorrect total still needed checking. It generated 27,970 reasoning tokens, and the response took 319.7 seconds—more than five minutes.

On the six questions that required adding up costs or durations across all 500 rows, Terra didn’t attempt an answer. It wrote a SQL query for me to run instead and marked each one as not calculated. Terra didn’t make up numbers, which is good. But it left the hardest part of the job, running the query and getting the totals, for you to do yourself. This is the first time I’ve seen AI hand work back.

Terra gave those answers with the same confidence as its correct ones, so nothing signaled that they were wrong. If you used those numbers in a report, you wouldn’t know which ones to double-check.

I’m including the numbers for both Terra and Astra here, but since the results were so different, the lower price and faster time aren’t wins.

  • Terra  133.1 s, 21,060 in, 11,554 out (10,707 reasoning), $0.079
  • Astra  319.7 s, 21,060 in, 28,806 out (27,970 reasoning), $1.65
Data validation

Astra scored a perfect 50, and Terra scored 45. 40 of the 50 points came from the 40 records that broke a rule. A model earned one point for each record it flagged, as long as it named the rule the record broke. The last 10 points came from records that looked wrong but followed every rule. A model lost a point for every correct record it accidentally flagged as incorrect.

The responses took 31.4 and 145.0 seconds, respectively; these elapsed times don’t isolate reasoning time.

Its 45/50 score is a test score, not an accuracy percentage across all 4,950 records. Three of the five it missed only break a rule when you compare them with other records in the file, such as a customer who reused another customer’s phone number. Terra flagged everything correctly, but it missed five invalid records. The results don’t explain why it missed them.

Astra caught all 40, but it took more than four times as long and cost about 12 times as much. Terra used fewer reasoning tokens and missed records in this run; that association does not establish the cause of the misses.

The numbers:

  • Terra  31.4 s, 234,045 in, 2,336 out (1,841 reasoning), $0.25
  • Astra  145.0 s, 234,045 in, 13,369 out (12,831 reasoning), $3.01

The numbers:

  • Terra  94.3 s, 251,651 in, 7,508 out (5,114 reasoning), $0.29
  • Astra  244.5 s, 251,651 in, 14,158 out (9,742 reasoning), $3.22
Results
TestTerra (out of 50)Astra (out of 50)GPT-5 Mini (out of 50)SQL reasoning26486Data validation455010Incident log triage505012Total (of 150)12114828Estimated token cost$0.61$7.88—Total time258.8 s709.2 s—

I included GPT-5 Mini’s baseline results for reference. I rebuilt these tests several times and kept making them harder because both models kept returning identical scores. Because I selected these harder versions after seeing earlier results, they shouldn’t be treated as a representative sample of everyday work. A low Mini score is a comparison point, not an independent measure of test difficulty. 

What do I think?

In these three final high-effort runs, Terra generated fewer reasoning tokens and finished sooner than Astra. It scored lower on SQL reasoning and data validation, and tied Astra on incident log triage. That is a trade-off in the results, but it doesn’t tell us whether Terra was overwhelmed or why it made specific errors. 

The measured totals were 258.8 seconds for Terra and 709.2 seconds for Astra, so Astra took about 2.74 times as long overall. At the stated standard uncached rates, the estimated token costs were $0.61 and $7.88; Terra’s cost was about 7.8% of Astra’s. Terra scored 121/150 and Astra 148/150 under these test rubrics. The runs show a cost, time, and score trade-off; they don’t show that OpenAI deliberately cut reasoning to achieve it. 

Terra matched Astra’s scores on my earlier easy and medium versions, but that does not establish its accuracy on every task at those difficulty levels. On the final tests, I would be cautious about using it for unchecked numerical aggregation or exhaustive data validation. It may be an acceptable lower-cost alternative for some workloads, including tasks like the incident triage tested here, as long as you verify the results. Astra’s incorrect SQL total also reminds you to check its work.

items.title: Democrats Trying to Get Hold of Trump’s Grok Conversations
items.summary: Ahead of the deadly airstrikes and military raid that saw US troops kidnap Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and deputy to the National Assembly Cilia Flores, Donald Trump was reportedly in the throes of a weeks-long mind meld with Grok. Elon Musk’s notorious generative AI chatbot had evidently convinced the president that he would be hailed as a hero for kidnapping the elected officials — a claim reinforced by widespread AI-generated misinformation on social media following the attack. Trump’s murderous assault on Caracas was successful, at least by the standards Grok cooked up. Now, however, the president’s obsession with the chatbot is becoming a major liability, as Democrats in the House judiciary and oversight committees demand the president’s chat logs be preserved for investigation. In a letter addressed to Trump, viewed by Politico , Democratic representatives Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia pressed the president to preserve “any prompts” given to AI chatbots like Grok while “carrying out your constitutional, statutory, or other official or ceremonial duties.” Any response from AI chatbots are likewise expected to be preserved. The letter asks for a briefing on the president’s use of large language models for executive decision making by November 11. According to Politico , the letter was triggered by reporting of Trump’s reliance on Grok to plan the January 3 attack on Caracas, which killed 100 people and left parts of the city in ruins . Specifically, Raskin and Garcia charged that Trump used Grok to “opine on how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro.” Based on the bot’s response, they say, Trump then “ordered the US military, without congressional authorization, to attack Venezuela and capture President Maduro.” How cooperative the notoriously churlish White House will be under Trump’s second term remains to be seen. In a statement shared by Politico , a White House official said that the “White House preserves all required records in accordance with the law” — though there’s no telling whether Trump will delete the logs himself following Grok’s advice. More on Trump: Trump Admin to Blast Immigrants With Heat-Ray Gun

items.title: Ingredients to Innovation: Computational Food Science with Wolfram
items.summary: In food science, small changes can have serious consequences. Altering an ingredient’s composition can affect its nutritional value and physical stability, while changing processing conditions can influence how a food behaves and whether it remains safe. The challenge is not simply measuring each effect in isolation but tracing how decisions about composition shape behavior during processing and storage. Wolfram makes those relationships computable within a unified environment. An investigation can begin with composition and extend into models of behavior under real conditions without being rebuilt at every turn. The resources in this guide show how that approach can support work in both academic and industrial settings. Analyzing Food Composition & Nutrition Composition is where many food-science questions begin. Curated food data in the Wolfram Knowledgebase makes nutritional properties directly computable, allowing users to compare foods quantitatively and identify differences that may shape the investigation that follows. Those results can provide a starting point for deeper work with experimental measurements or questions about formulation and molecular behavior. Comparing amino acid profiles can reveal differences among potential protein sources and help frame questions for further nutritional investigation. Featured Resource: AminoAcidsBarChart Two foods can contain similar amounts of protein while differing in the amounts of individual amino acids they provide. The Wolfram Function Repository function AminoAcidsBarChart uses curated food data to make those differences visible. The chart can compare any one of 20 amino acids across a selection of foods, updating as the choices change. Users can examine one property across several foods or narrow the comparison to the foods most relevant to a particular question. Here, the chart displays the relative alanine content of several high-protein foods, providing an accessible starting point for investigating how nutritional composition connects with the molecular questions explored in the next section: Because users can change the foods being compared, the visualization can be adapted to new questions without rebuilding the analysis. This makes it useful for both guided classroom exploration and preliminary nutritional comparisons. Explore More FoodCompassPlot — Visually summarize the nutritional composition of an individual food or a complete recipe as percentages of recommended daily values. NutritionReport — Generate a structured nutritional summary for a food or recipe. EntityValue — Retrieve specified nutritional and other curated properties from computable Food entities in the Wolfram Knowledgebase. Exploring Food Chemistry & Molecular Structure Nutritional composition describes what a food contains, but molecular structure provides another way to investigate how its components differ. Representing food-related compounds as computable molecules allows researchers and students to compare structural features, visualize chemical differences and frame questions for further experimental study. Quantifying molecular similarity can help researchers identify chemically related compounds for closer investigation before experimental testing. Featured Resource: MoleculeFeatureDistance Fatty acids can share the same basic carbon-chain architecture while differing in the number of carbon–carbon double bonds they contain. MoleculeFeatureDistance provides a computational way to compare those structures by measuring the distance between their molecular features. Here, the function was applied pairwise to stearic, oleic, linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids. The resulting heat map shows smaller distances between molecules with more similar structural features. According to this molecular-feature measure, oleic and linoleic acids form the most similar pair in the comparison, while stearic and alpha-linolenic acids are the most dissimilar. These values describe similarity between molecular features; they do not by themselves predict nutritional effects, physical behavior or suitability as ingredient substitutes. They can, however, provide a quantitative starting point for exploring relationships among chemically related food components. Explore More MoleculeView — Explore computable molecular structures through coordinated 2D and interactive 3D representations. MoleculeValue — Retrieve molecular properties to compare the characteristics of food-related compounds. MoleculeSubstructure — Represent selected atoms and bonds within a molecule to examine specific structural features. Modeling Food Processing, Safety & Stability Understanding what a food contains is only the first part of the problem; scientists also need to know how it changes. During processing and storage, operating conditions can reshape a food’s physical behavior and alter the point at which its quality or safety becomes unacceptable. Computational models make those changes explorable, providing a bridge between general scientific principles and product-specific testing. Featured Resource: Estimation of Time to Excessive Microbial Count Microbial counts in foods and water can fluctuate irregularly, making it difficult to judge when they might reach a specified upper limit. Statistical modeling offers one way to investigate that uncertainty by estimating how frequently a specified threshold might be exceeded. The Estimation of Time to Excessive Microbial Count Demonstration generates repeated Monte Carlo simulations using a lognormal, normal, log-Laplace or Laplace distribution. Users can work with hypothetical or experimentally determined parameters, set the microbial-count threshold and examine when each simulated series first crosses it. The resulting histogram shows the distribution of those first-exceedance times, providing a way to explore how soon an excessive count might occur if conditions remain unchanged. The model assumes that successive counts are independent, with no underlying trend or periodicity. Its results therefore illustrate probabilistic threshold analysis rather than microbial growth or a product-specific safety determination. Explore More Hysteresis in the Flow Curves of Pseudoplastic Semiliquid Foods — Explore how a semiliquid food’s apparent viscosity and flow behavior change as shear conditions increase and decrease. “ How Long to Boil an Egg? FEM Modeling with Wolfram Language ” — Use finite element modeling to investigate heat transfer during cooking and predict how temperature changes inside an egg. Vitamin C Loss in Foods during Heat Processing and Storage — Model how heating and storage conditions influence vitamin C degradation over time. Applying Food Science Data in Research and R&D Food science research begins with measurements, but its real value lies in finding the relationships those measurements reveal. Statistical tools can expose patterns within experimental data, while adjustable mathematical models allow researchers to test how food quality or microbial survival might change under different conditions. These resources show how Wolfram methods can carry an investigation from data analysis toward the questions that shape academic research and industrial R&D. Featured Resource: Correlation and Regression Analysis of Meat Fat Content Food researchers often need to determine whether measured characteristics vary together and how different mathematical models might describe their relationship. The Wolfram Language Example Repository example Correlation and Regression Analysis of Meat Fat Content uses Correlation to measure associations among nutritional properties of meats, then applies ListFitPlot to visualize linear, exponential and local regression fits to the resulting data. A straight line is a useful first pass, not a verdict. Here, the red line summarizes the relationship between saturated and monounsaturated fat across the selected meats, while the surrounding band shows the 95% confidence interval for that fit. Because real food data rarely behaves with perfect obedience, the same measurements can also be tested against exponential or locally smoothed models, allowing researchers to compare different descriptions of the pattern before deciding what deserves closer investigation. Explore More Reaction Rate Dependence on Temperature and Moisture during Storage — Model how temperature and moisture content jointly influence reaction rates in stored dried foods and visualize the relationship in three dimensions. Probabilistic Model for Microbial Mortality — Simulate microbial survival as a stochastic process and examine how population size and mortality probabilities affect the resulting survival curve. Multiple-Effect Evaporation of Sugar Solution — Compare single- and multiple-effect evaporation of a sugar solution by adjusting feed flow rate and pressure. Computational Food Science in the Classroom The same computational methods used to investigate food composition, behavior and experimental data can also give students models they can inspect, modify and test for themselves. Wolfram U courses and downloadable notebooks provide that starting point, helping students move from familiar questions about food toward reproducible investigations using computable data. Featured Resource: Wolfram U’s Computational Food and Nutrition The beginner-level Computational Food and Nutrition course provides 75 minutes of instruction led by a registered dietitian. Its three videos move from retrieving and organizing computable food data to visualization and statistical analysis, showing how questions about nutrition can become reproducible computational investigations. Downloadable course notebooks give instructors working material that can be adapted for demonstrations or assignments, while students gain experience querying Wolfram’s food knowledgebase and analyzing the resulting data. The course therefore offers more than an overview of available functionality: it provides a structured starting point for bringing computation into food science and nutrition instruction. Explore More Wolfram|Alpha Food Science — Explore food composition, nutrition and the physical principles of cooking through accessible natural language queries and calculations. Wolfram Language Example Repository Food & Nutrition — Browse and adapt 16 ready-to-use Wolfram Language notebooks spanning nutritional analysis and the chemical or physical behavior of foods. “ Should I Eat That? Food Science and Safety with the Wolfram Language ” — See how Wolfram food data can support nutritional analysis and investigations of food storage, safety and foodborne illness. Carrying the Investigation Forward Food science rarely stops at a single measurement. A difference in composition can raise molecular questions, change processing behavior or alter what must be tested for safety and stability. Making those connections computable allows an investigation to follow the consequences as they emerge instead of treating each stage as a separate problem. The resources collected here are starting points rather than fixed recipes. They give users in academic and industrial settings reproducible methods that can be adapted as the data, assumptions and scientific questions change. That flexibility allows computation to move food science beyond description and toward a deeper understanding of how food behaves in the real world.
