items.title: Intel plunges more than 25% amid surging memory costs and PC weakness
items.summary: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned of one of the "most significant supply shortages in history." Akio Kon/Bloomberg via Getty Images Intel shares dropped more than 25% on Friday after disappointing earnings. The chipmaker said it expects revenue to drop in Q4 as its PC business faces headwinds. Computing is facing "one of the most significant supply shortages in history," its CEO said. Intel shares plummeted 28% on Friday after the chipmaker warned about a weaker market as supply shortages linked to the AI boom bite. Shares in the California-headquartered company were trading at $65.79 soon after the open, down from $92.07 at Thursday's close. On Thursday, it reported third-quarter revenue of $16.5 billion, up 20% from a year earlier. However, it forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and earnings per share of $0.25 — down from $0.52 in the third quarter. The AI boom is increasing demand for memory and server chips needed to train and run AI models, creating shortages that have pushed up memory prices. That makes PCs more expensive to build and buy, prompting computer-makers to order fewer Intel chips. "The industry continues to navigate one of the most significant supply shortages in history, driven by the unprecedented demand for super intelligence," Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on Thursday's earnings call. Intel's client-computing group, which sells chips for PCs, generated $8.1 billion in the third quarter, down 9% from the previous quarter. The company said it expects the division's revenue to decline by more than 20% in the fourth quarter. Intel's share price has boomed in 2026, climbing more than 130% as of Thursday's close. That rise has stalled in recent weeks amid a wider sell-off in the tech sector. After Friday's open, its year-to-date rise is around 67%. Friday's sharp drop comes during a busy earnings week, with other tech firms also reporting disappointing numbers. On Thursday, Google recorded the largest single-day market cap loss in its history, shedding $500 billion in value after worse-than-expected revenue from its AI search tool pushed shares down 12%. Chip shortages hit home Intel said higher memory prices and limited availability were making computers more expensive. It expects global PC sales to decline about 12% this year, and by roughly another 10% in 2027. "We do not expect a sustained recovery until memory availability improves and pricing begins to normalize," said Dave Zinsner, the chief financial officer. The company's data-center business offered some hope, with revenue up nearly 80% year over year to $7.3 billion. However, Intel said it could not meet all the demand for its server chips. It cited a two-week shutdown at its Israeli plant following what Tan called "an unfortunate and tragic accident," which it expects to cut fourth-quarter revenue by about $300 million. items.title: Lessons from Barry Diller, Ashley Graham, and Strauss Zelnick: Here are the biggest takeaways from BI's The Long Play
items.summary: Carl Timpone/BFA This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . A media mogul billionaire, a supermodel, and a unicorn founder walk into a conference. Welcome to life at The Long Play . BI's big event in NYC, which I had the honor of hosting, featured leaders from across the business spectrum. From AI infrastructure and healthcare to video games and publishing, we had it all covered. You'd think such a wide-ranging group would be facing very different challenges. And on a granular level, they are. Carolyn Tisch Blodgett's daily efforts to gain support for Gotham FC are very different from John Santora's day-to-day work turning around WeWork. But one big takeaway I had from the day — and something I heard repeatedly from people I spoke with at the event — is that the big-picture challenges are the same. And hearing how top leaders are navigating them was incredibly helpful. Maybe that's growing your business in the face of some political surprises (Nubank cofounder Cristina Junqueira ). Maybe it's pivoting a company to lean into the AI era (CEO of Allbirds-turned-Smartbird Nadia Carlsten ). Or maybe it's just about taking the right steps to stay healthy in your daily life (Take-Two Interactive CEO and chairman Strauss Zelnick ). After all, we're all thinking about the long play. Here are some other big stories from the day: Barry Diller weighs in on his MGM deal. The media mogul believes real-world experiences are the strongest hedge against AI, which is why his company People Inc. tried to buy MGM in June. At BI's The Long Play, Diller shared why the deal ultimately fell apart and why he has no plans to retire at the age of 84 . The room was full of schmoozing and musing. Our reporter Henry Chandonnet networked with founders fine-tuning pitches, contemplating the future of work, and sharing laughs from their seats at The Long Play. From the hot takes to the aha moments and surprisingly (in Henry's words!) good food, see what it was like in the room . From history-making supermodel to leading a brand empire. Ashley Graham's career spans from being the first-ever plus-size model on the cover of Sports Illustrated to building a business portfolio. She shared why raising money for her alcohol brand was "very, very hard and humbling." You can watch her discuss vision boarding and how rejection has made her better in business with BI's Leena Rao . The guy behind one of gaming's most anticipated releases has some health advice. Strauss Zelnick leads the company behind Grand Theft Auto, but he keeps some simple, healthy habits. He shared the eight he lives by and why peptides aren't one of them . And much like his health regimen, Zelnick prefers a clear-cut management style , prioritizing direct CEO access and avoiding "toxic" discretionary pay programs. Also at The Long Play: Nubank, Latin America's largest digital bank, is turning its eyes toward the US — where foreign rivals have failed. Plus, watch Nubank's co-founder share her fintech success story . How a co-owner of the New York Giants is using AI to build a women's sports powerhouse with Gotham FC . She also explained why bringing your whole self to work can mean bringing your kids , too. WeWork CEO explains how a dress code and RTO flexibility helped change the culture at the once-troubled company. Smartbird's CEO talks about converting a shoe company into an AI player . Read the original article on Business Insider

You'd think such a wide-ranging group would be facing very different challenges. And on a granular level, they are. Carolyn Tisch Blodgett's daily efforts to gain support for Gotham FC are very different from John Santora's day-to-day work turning around WeWork.

But one big takeaway I had from the day — and something I heard repeatedly from people I spoke with at the event — is that the big-picture challenges are the same. And hearing how top leaders are navigating them was incredibly helpful.

Maybe that's growing your business in the face of some political surprises (Nubank cofounder Cristina Junqueira). Maybe it's pivoting a company to lean into the AI era (CEO of Allbirds-turned-Smartbird Nadia Carlsten). Or maybe it's just about taking the right steps to stay healthy in your daily life (Take-Two Interactive CEO and chairman Strauss Zelnick).

After all, we're all thinking about the long play.

Here are some other big stories from the day:

Barry Diller weighs in on his MGM deal. The media mogul believes real-world experiences are the strongest hedge against AI, which is why his company People Inc. tried to buy MGM in June. At BI's The Long Play, Diller shared why the deal ultimately fell apart and why he has no plans to retire at the age of 84.

The room was full of schmoozing and musing. Our reporter Henry Chandonnet networked with founders fine-tuning pitches, contemplating the future of work, and sharing laughs from their seats at The Long Play. He shared the eight he lives by and why peptides aren't one of them. And much like his health regimen, Zelnick prefers a clear-cut management style, prioritizing direct CEO access and avoiding "toxic" discretionary pay programs.

items.title: The Download: GLP-1s and eating disorders, self-aware cities, and forever chemicals

GLP-1s could make things worse. GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinicians, they can represent something sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders. A new report suggests the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up by 71% between 1990 and 2023. And clinicians are already seeing GLP-1s exacerbate the issue. Here’s how they could make an already growing problem worse . —Jessica Hamzelou This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. Love is infrastructure —“Love is Infrastructure” is a short fictional story by Charlie Jane Anders, author of a forthcoming novel titled Good Things Are Coming Your Way . Mainspring and St. Barnabas are two neighboring cities with different personalities. They’ve never particularly liked each other, but that changes when both develop minds of their own, shaped by the votes of their residents. As the cities begin to fall for each other, a third city enters the picture. Turnbull promises Mainspring a more efficient future, but its vision of urban life comes with a troubling price. Read the full short story about self-aware cities, direct democracy, and a steamy romance. This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine . Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. Are we there yet? Cleaning up PFAS Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” are linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. Scrubbing PFAS-contaminated soil could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. The concept is still in its infancy, but we can limit their buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. Find out how close we are to ridding the world of forever chemicals . —Sara Kiley Watson This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue . This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.

GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinicians, they can represent something sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.

A new report suggests the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up by 71% between 1990 and 2023. And clinicians are already seeing GLP-1s exacerbate the issue.

Here’s how they could make an already growing problem worse.

—Jessica Hamzelou

This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

Love is infrastructure

—“Love is Infrastructure” is a short fictional story by Charlie Jane Anders, author of a forthcoming novel titled Good Things Are Coming Your Way.

Mainspring and St. Barnabas are two neighboring cities with different personalities. They’ve never particularly liked each other, but that changes when both develop minds of their own, shaped by the votes of their residents.

As the cities begin to fall for each other, a third city enters the picture. Turnbull promises Mainspring a more efficient future, but its vision of urban life comes with a troubling price.

Read the full short story about self-aware cities, direct democracy, and a steamy romance.

This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.

Are we there yet? Cleaning up PFAS 

Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” are linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. 

Scrubbing PFAS-contaminated soil could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. The concept is still in its infancy, but we can limit their buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. 


Find out how close we are to ridding the world of forever chemicals.

items.title: Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push
items.summary: Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question. Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech. The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count. AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning. The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019. Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.” Notable deals Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States. The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews , which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth , with participation from Atomico , HarbourVest Partners , Kinnevik , Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management . The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion. Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities , joined by New Alliance Capital , Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely , develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis. Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue. Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field , bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million. Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo , which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital , Isai and Ternel . The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments. Exits Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities. Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets , a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February. On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November. Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing. Related Crunchbase query: Funding To Travel-Related Startups Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: Don’t trust AI to keep your secrets
items.summary: We talk to chatbots as if those conversations are private. But are they? Most people are confused. A survey commissioned by DuckDuckGo and published in August asked 1,944 American adults about chatbot privacy, and more than half (53%) did not know whether their conversations were being used to train the bots. (They are.) Only a quarter of respondents knew that chatbot conversations can be subpoenaed. (They can.) Among self-described AI enthusiasts, 56% said they had confided to a chatbot something they had never told a close friend, parent, colleague, doctor, or therapist. That’s especially true on Character.AI, a chatbot service where users can chat and form “relationships” with customizable characters, including ones they create and share with the community. On Character.AI, some users chat about thoughts of suicide and self-harm, and they surrender private details like mental health disclosures, ages, private chats and voice calls, deep fears, and relationship struggles. Character.AI was all fun and games until earlier this month, when the company filed for bankruptcy and opened a court-supervised sale of its assets. Nobody knows who will end up with the company, or how much of the data on its millions of account holders will be sold as well. The most valuable asset for sale by the company may be its LLM, which has been substantially trained by users as they build and interact with characters. Legally, a company can sell personal data about its users if its privacy policy permits the transfer. Character.AI’s privacy policy is spectacularly vague. It says the company may disclose “certain information” in the company’s sale. Nobody knows what that means. The US Trustee Office, an arm of the Justice Department, wants the judge to appoint a consumer privacy ombudsman to advise the court on user privacy. The judge could restrict the sale of company “records,” including user data. But here’s the part most people don’t understand: The Bankruptcy Code has no provision specifically addressing trained models. The legal status of LLMs and their training data has yet to be settled in law. That means it’s entirely possible that the data users fed into Character.AI will be sold to whoever buys it. Character.AI is just one handy example. The larger risk is all the other AI companies out there. More surprising facts about LLM privacy The core question is this: Can personal or proprietary information shared in a chat end up inside an LLM, where anyone might coax it out? The answer is a resounding “uh, maybe.” First of all, it depends on the AI chatbot service. The companies vary wildly in how they handle chat data, and the differences boil down to four questions: whether training on chats is on by default, whether human reviewers read them, how long they are kept, and whether they feed advertising. Major chatbot companies generally try to reassure users about privacy. They publish privacy controls, but their own policies admit that consumer chats may be used for training by default, read by human reviewers, or both, and the fine print shifts from company to company. Tellingly, some of them offer enterprise or business accounts that handle chat sessions privately. For example, they don’t use chat sessions in training data. That business accounts get extra privacy features sounds to me like an admission that individual accounts aren’t private. Some companies, such as OpenAI, let users opt out of having their chats tossed into the training data. But OpenAI’s help documentation says that turning off training does not delete the chats themselves. There are three main ways chatbot user data can be exposed. The first is bugs. In March 2023, a bug lurking in an open-source library called “redis-py” let some ChatGPT users see other users’ chat titles and, possibly, the first message of new conversations. More than 1% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window may have had their payment details exposed to other users: names, email addresses, payment addresses, card types, the last four digits of card numbers and expiration dates. The second is sharing. Some chatbots offer sharing features, and those features can publish chats to the world, whether on purpose or by accident. Once these sessions are posted, search engines are likely to gobble them up and make them searchable. In 2025, Forbes reported that Google’s results showed more than 370,000 Grok conversations after users clicked “share,” and shared ChatGPT chats turned up in search results until OpenAI killed the option. The third is the absorption of chat sessions into the training data. Let’s take one simple example: an email address. People often paste in emails so that a chatbot will write the reply. These emails often contain names, email addresses and other information in the header, the signature, or both. The question I often ponder is this: If emails addressed to one person get pasted into chats hundreds of times, can a stranger ask the chatbot for that person’s address and actually get it back? In a 2022 study , GPT-Neo models given only a person’s name recovered the right email address no more than 1.24% of the time, but with the domain supplied, the rate climbed to 16.55%, and to 37.06% after five examples. Other factors, including how often an address appeared in the training data and whether surrounding email text came along with it, pushed the rate higher. Deleting chat records isn’t a remedy, either. Several state attorneys general said deleting chat records may not undo their influence on trained models. And Common Sense Media’s Robbie Torney claimed that exporting or deleting your data “may not mean that that data is gone from model training.” Note that people not only enter personal information about themselves during AI chats, but about their co-workers, friends, and relatives. The main thing standing between your secrets and the world is company practice. We depend on the AI companies to keep our information private. So what happens when those companies sell their assets? When AI bubbles burst Online chatter about the “AI bubble” bursting is pretty much constant. In China, the AI bubble has already burst, according to Reuters . Over the past few months, Chinese AI stocks have been pummeled. Reuters reported that Shanghai’s STAR50 index of tech stocks fell 40% from its July high in under four months, erasing about $480 billion in market value, and that the broader CSI300 is down about 20% from its June highs. It’s not a total collapse, but it does put pressure on US stock prices and also provides an incentive to transfer ownership through sales or mergers (though this hasn’t happened in China yet). Still, the future is unknowable. Which AI companies will go bust as Character.AI did, get sold off, or get hacked? As for the chatbots themselves, their inner workings are also unknowable. That’s why we should all listen to the most paranoid amongst us, and never put sensitive information into chatbots. We just can’t trust AI to keep our secrets.

The core question is this: Can personal or proprietary information shared in a chat end up inside an LLM, where anyone might coax it out?

The answer is a resounding “uh, maybe.”

First of all, it depends on the AI chatbot service. The companies vary wildly in how they handle chat data, and the differences boil down to four questions: whether training on chats is on by default, whether human reviewers read them, how long they are kept, and whether they feed advertising.

Major chatbot companies generally try to reassure users about privacy. They publish privacy controls, but their own policies admit that consumer chats may be used for training by default, read by human reviewers, or both, and the fine print shifts from company to company.

Tellingly, some of them offer enterprise or business accounts that handle chat sessions privately. For example, they don’t use chat sessions in training data. That business accounts get extra privacy features sounds to me like an admission that individual accounts aren’t private.

Some companies, such as OpenAI, let users opt out of having their chats tossed into the training data. But OpenAI’s help documentation says that turning off training does not delete the chats themselves.

There are three main ways chatbot user data can be exposed. The first is bugs. In March 2023, a bug lurking in an open-source library called “redis-py” let some ChatGPT users see other users’ chat titles and, possibly, the first message of new conversations. More than 1% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window may have had their payment details exposed to other users: names, email addresses, payment addresses, card types, the last four digits of card numbers and expiration dates.

The second is sharing. Some chatbots offer sharing features, and those features can publish chats to the world, whether on purpose or by accident. Once these sessions are posted, search engines are likely to gobble them up and make them searchable. In 2025, Forbes reported that Google’s results showed more than 370,000 Grok conversations after users clicked “share,” and shared ChatGPT chats turned up in search results until OpenAI killed the option.

The third is the absorption of chat sessions into the training data.

Let’s take one simple example: an email address. People often paste in emails so that a chatbot will write the reply. These emails often contain names, email addresses and other information in the header, the signature, or both.

The question I often ponder is this: If emails addressed to one person get pasted into chats hundreds of times, can a stranger ask the chatbot for that person’s address and actually get it back?

In a 2022 study, GPT-Neo models given only a person’s name recovered the right email address no more than 1.24% of the time, but with the domain supplied, the rate climbed to 16.55%, and to 37.06% after five examples. Other factors, including how often an address appeared in the training data and whether surrounding email text came along with it, pushed the rate higher.

Deleting chat records isn’t a remedy, either. Several state attorneys general said deleting chat records may not undo their influence on trained models. And Common Sense Media’s Robbie Torney claimed that exporting or deleting your data “may not mean that that data is gone from model training.”

Note that people not only enter personal information about themselves during AI chats, but about their co-workers, friends, and relatives.

The main thing standing between your secrets and the world is company practice. We depend on the AI companies to keep our information private.

So what happens when those companies sell their assets?

When AI bubbles burst

Online chatter about the “AI bubble” bursting is pretty much constant.

In China, the AI bubble has already burst, according to Reuters. Over the past few months, Chinese AI stocks have been pummeled.

Reuters reported that Shanghai’s STAR50 index of tech stocks fell 40% from its July high in under four months, erasing about $480 billion in market value, and that the broader CSI300 is down about 20% from its June highs.

It’s not a total collapse, but it does put pressure on US stock prices and also provides an incentive to transfer ownership through sales or mergers (though this hasn’t happened in China yet).

Still, the future is unknowable. Which AI companies will go bust as Character.AI did, get sold off, or get hacked?

As for the chatbots themselves, their inner workings are also unknowable.

That’s why we should all listen to the most paranoid amongst us, and never put sensitive information into chatbots. We just can’t trust AI to keep our secrets.

items.title: AIhub monthly digest: October 2026 – neurosymbolic planning, time-series forecasting, and robots for the home
items.summary: Welcome to our monthly digest, where you can catch up with any AIhub stories you may have missed, peruse the latest news, recap recent events, and more. This month, we chat to AI pioneer, Michael Littman, learn about time-series forecasting for clinical data, investigate evolutionary game theory for cybersecurity, and get the scoop on neuromorphic computing. From teaching machines to teaching people: an interview with Michael Littman In the latest interview in our series meeting AI pioneers, Michael Littman reflects on the evolution of reinforcement learning, the power of science communication, and how generative AI is changing the way we teach and learn. Machine learning for clinical time-series forecasting Mayra Elwes is a PhD student developing machine learning methods for clinical time-series data. She is working on practical strategies to evaluate methods in a more contextualised way and on improving existing domain adaptation methods specific to time-series forecasting. We caught up with Mayra to find out more. Cybersecurity and evolutionary game theory Adeela Bashir is working at the intersection of cybersecurity, evolutionary game theory, and AI safety. We heard from Adeela about her PhD, in which she is focussed on the question: how can we understand and mitigate cyber threats when the adversaries are adaptive? In other words, can AI defend itself when the attackers are evolving too? Competing in RoboCup@Home and winning the 2026 best paper award Raphael Memmesheimer has long been competing in the RoboCup@Home league winning the RoboCup@Home competition five times. He and his colleagues took home the best paper award at RoboCup 2026 for their work Efficient Image Annotation via Semi-Supervised Object Segmentation with Label Propagation . We chatted up with Raphael to find out more about this research, his history with RoboCup, and the challenges of the @Home competition. Neurosymbolic planning using natural language communication for cooperative autonomous vehicles In this blog post , Neel P. Bhatt, Po-han Li, Kushagra Gupta, Ufuk Topcu and David Fridovich-Keil write about their research on neurosymbolic planning using natural language communication for cooperative autonomous vehicles. This work was nominated for the AAMAS 2026 best paper award. Vision language models and the physical world At ICML 2026 , Dezhi Luo, Yijiang Li, Maijunxian Wang, Tianwei Zhao, Bingyang Wang, Siheng Wang, Pinyuan Feng, Pooyan Rahmanzadehgervi, Ziqiao Ma and Hokin Deng presented their work Vision Language Models Cannot Reason About Physical Transformation . In this interview, William Yijiang Li tells us more about the research, the method the team used, and the controlled experiments they carried out. Rebuilding the brain with neuromorphic computing What can we learn from the brain about building better computers? Oliver Rhodes discusses how neuromorphic computing draws on the brain’s architecture to develop new approaches to more efficient information processing. Credit fairness: lending resources without losing out In their paper presented at IJCAI-ECAI 2026 , Seyed Majid Zahedi and Rupert Freeman investigate repeated allocation of shared resources among agents. They introduce credit fairness, a property that strengthens sharing incentives. Read their blog post to find out more. AAAI/SIGAI Doctoral Consortium interview collection Each year, a small group of PhD students are chosen to participate in the AAAI/SIGAI Doctoral Consortium. This initiative provides an opportunity for the students to discuss and explore their research interests and career objectives in an interdisciplinary workshop together with a panel of established researchers. During 2026, we met with 15 of these students to find out more about their research. We’ve collated all of these interviews here . AI, ethics and society in Sweden The ninth AAAI / ACM Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Society (AIES) took place in Malmö, Sweden from 12-14 October 2026. The programme included keynote talks, a panel, discussion sessions, paper presentations, and posters. We cast an eye over social media to find out what the participants got up to . Look out for blog posts from some of the presenters who will be writing about work they brought to the conference. 2027 ACM SIGAI Autonomous Agents Research Award open for nominations Nominations are solicited for the 2027 ACM SIGAI Autonomous Agents Research Award . This award is made for excellence in research in the area of autonomous agents. It is intended to recognize researchers whose current work is an important influence on the field. items.summary_html:
Welcome to our monthly digest, where you can catch up with any AIhub stories you may have missed, peruse the latest news, recap recent events, and more. This month, we chat to AI pioneer, Michael Littman, learn about time-series forecasting for clinical data, investigate evolutionary game theory for cybersecurity, and get the scoop on neuromorphic computing.

From teaching machines to teaching people: an interview with Michael Littman

In the latest interview in our series meeting AI pioneers, Michael Littman reflects on the evolution of reinforcement learning, the power of science communication, and how generative AI is changing the way we teach and learn.

Machine learning for clinical time-series forecasting

Mayra Elwes is a PhD student developing machine learning methods for clinical time-series data. She is working on practical strategies to evaluate methods in a more contextualised way and on improving existing domain adaptation methods specific to time-series forecasting. We caught up with Mayra to find out more.

Cybersecurity and evolutionary game theory

Adeela Bashir is working at the intersection of cybersecurity, evolutionary game theory, and AI safety. We heard from Adeela about her PhD, in which she is focussed on the question: how can we understand and mitigate cyber threats when the adversaries are adaptive? In other words, can AI defend itself when the attackers are evolving too?

Competing in RoboCup@Home and winning the 2026 best paper award

Raphael Memmesheimer has long been competing in the RoboCup@Home league winning the RoboCup@Home competition five times. He and his colleagues took home the best paper award at RoboCup 2026 for their work Efficient Image Annotation via Semi-Supervised Object Segmentation with Label Propagation. We chatted up with Raphael to find out more about this research, his history with RoboCup, and the challenges of the @Home competition.

Neurosymbolic planning using natural language communication for cooperative autonomous vehicles

In this blog post, Neel P. Bhatt, Po-han Li, Kushagra Gupta, Ufuk Topcu and David Fridovich-Keil write about their research on neurosymbolic planning using natural language communication for cooperative autonomous vehicles. This work was nominated for the AAMAS 2026 best paper award.

Vision language models and the physical world

At ICML 2026, Dezhi Luo, Yijiang Li, Maijunxian Wang, Tianwei Zhao, Bingyang Wang, Siheng Wang, Pinyuan Feng, Pooyan Rahmanzadehgervi, Ziqiao Ma and Hokin Deng presented their work Vision Language Models Cannot Reason About Physical Transformation. In this interview, William Yijiang Li tells us more about the research, the method the team used, and the controlled experiments they carried out.

Rebuilding the brain with neuromorphic computing

What can we learn from the brain about building better computers? Oliver Rhodes discusses how neuromorphic computing draws on the brain’s architecture to develop new approaches to more efficient information processing.

Credit fairness: lending resources without losing out

In their paper presented at IJCAI-ECAI 2026, Seyed Majid Zahedi and Rupert Freeman investigate repeated allocation of shared resources among agents. They introduce credit fairness, a property that strengthens sharing incentives. Read their blog post to find out more.

AAAI/SIGAI Doctoral Consortium interview collection

Each year, a small group of PhD students are chosen to participate in the AAAI/SIGAI Doctoral Consortium. This initiative provides an opportunity for the students to discuss and explore their research interests and career objectives in an interdisciplinary workshop together with a panel of established researchers. During 2026, we met with 15 of these students to find out more about their research. We’ve collated all of these interviews here.

AI, ethics and society in Sweden

The ninth AAAI / ACM Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Society (AIES) took place in Malmö, Sweden from 12-14 October 2026. The programme included keynote talks, a panel, discussion sessions, paper presentations, and posters. We cast an eye over social media to find out what the participants got up to. Look out for blog posts from some of the presenters who will be writing about work they brought to the conference.

2027 ACM SIGAI Autonomous Agents Research Award open for nominations

Nominations are solicited for the 2027 ACM SIGAI Autonomous Agents Research Award. This award is made for excellence in research in the area of autonomous agents. It is intended to recognize researchers whose current work is an important influence on the field. Find out how to nominate here.

items.title: Inside the spy plot around Nvidia’s CEO
items.summary: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,617 new readers. Nvidia’s chips are at the center of the U.S.-China AI race, and Washington has spent years trying to keep the best ones out of Beijing’s hands. Now, a New York Times report says U.S. intelligence found that an alleged Chinese asset had built close ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang… and the White House chose not to act. In today’s AI rundown: Report: Nvidia CEO targeted by alleged Chinese spy Rowan’s Corner: ‘Sent from my agent’ Make ElevenLabs voiceovers sound more natural Anthropic’s AI now monitors its own conversations LATEST DEVELOPMENTS NVIDIA 🕵️ Report: Nvidia CEO targeted by alleged Chinese spy Image source: Net Thunder on LinkedIn The Rundown: The NYT just reported that U.S. officials found Alice Huang, an exec at Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed, was allegedly passing intelligence to Beijing while keeping close ties with Jensen Huang, with Trump briefed about a year ago. The details: It’s unclear what Ms. Huang passed to Beijing or its value, but officials worried she could offer insight into Trump’s view on chip sales to China, and into Nvidia itself. Officials didn’t believe Jensen knew of her alleged role when Trump was briefed; he never got a defensive briefing, often given to U.S. citizens targeted by spies. Megaspeed, already under U.S. probe for steering Nvidia chips to China, bought at least $4.8B in Nvidia gear via a sister firm, and remains an Nvidia cloud partner. Nvidia called Jensen’s meetings with Ms. Huang routine, saying customers get ordinary business info and “zero information relevant to national security.” Megaspeed said outside counsel is investigating and it’s cooperating with the U.S., while China called the claims “groundless smears and slanders.” Why it matters: The report reads like a spy thriller, but nothing has been publicly proven, including whether Ms. Huang passed anything to China. The immediate fallout may hit the loophole allowing firms like Megaspeed to rent Nvidia-powered computing from Southeast Asia to Chinese AI labs — one Trump reopened but may now close. TOGETHER WITH OPENART 🧑‍🎨 Create a launch video for your business The Rundown: Need a launch video for your business? Simply paste your website link, add your brand assets, and define your target audience. OpenArt’s AI video agent will shape the story and messaging while handling the script, motion design, voiceover, and video editing. With OpenArt, you can: Turn your website, screenshots, or pitch deck into a launch video Create short promos or longer videos to showcase your business Refine scenes, voiceovers, or music by describing the changes Go beyond launches with product ads and UGC-style videos Create your launch video with OpenArt . ROWAN’S CORNER 🤖 ‘Sent from my agent’ h/t to @gregisenberg for the tweet Rowan: “Sent from my agent” is becoming the new “Sent from iPhone.” That’s a tweet my friend Greg Isenberg recently made that’s stirring up conversation. Basically, “Sent from my iPhone” started as a way to buy forgiveness for typos and messy formatting when emailing someone from your iPhone. But when someone sees “Sent from my agent,” the real message they receive is: you weren’t worth my attention . There’s real tension here (for me included). Agents are the biggest leverage available right now, and I run several tasks through them, saving me at least a few hours a week. But I also believe going the extra mile and writing something yourself shows the other human respect. So here’s my line: Anything that touches a person is me — social posts, messages, recruiting calls, live video. Anything that’s a task, an agent can do. I also have a growing thesis that real human relationships will only become more valuable as AI gets better. Anything that risks that trust is probably a bad trade. Personally, if I see “sent from my agent,” I’m deleting the email. I’ve written before that AI intuition is the most important skill of this decade, knowing which tasks to hand to AI, and this is the perfect example. Use agents everywhere, except on people. Are you using agents to respond to your emails, or do you think the human touch shows respect? Let me know in the poll at the bottom of the email. I’m curious! AI TRAINING 🎙️ Make ElevenLabs voiceovers sound more natural The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll add Audio Tags to a short Eleven v4 voiceover, compare it with the plain version, and create a short scene with two speakers. Step-by-step: Open ElevenLabs Text to Speech, choose one voice, and select Eleven v4. Generate the guide’s plain script and save it for comparison Paste the tagged version without changing the spoken words. Keep the same voice and settings so you can hear the difference Compare the opening, pace, and final line. If the delivery stays flat, make one cue more specific. Change one thing at a time If a tag gets read aloud, check the model and square brackets. Keep the direction short and place it before the words it should affect Open Dialogue mode, add two voices, and generate the guide’s exchange. Check the words, speakers, and timing before downloading the clips Pro tip: Save a plain version before adding tags. A more expressive read may still sound less natural. You can find our full cheat sheet, annotated scripts, and review checklist here . PRESENTED BY GLEAN 🚀 From data to decisions, faster The Rundown: Business data spans across apps, warehouses, and BI platforms, while the context behind the numbers lives in documents, tickets, and conversations. Glean’s upcoming webinar helps you bring it all together, find trusted answers, and make data-driven decisions without SQL or a BI background. In this webinar, you’ll learn how to: Query business data in natural language Quickly build dashboards to track key metrics Connect metrics with enterprise context Register for the webinar and put AI to work . ANTHROPIC / AI SAFETY 🚨 Anthropic’s AI now monitors its own conversations Image source: Anthropic The Rundown: Anthropic introduced “self-assessment,” a technique where Claude reviews the chat after each reply and flags potential misuse, saying the system has been active since June and catching large-scale abuse that might otherwise be missed. The details: Claude gives each conversation a quick safety verdict (whether it’s harmful, what kind of harm, and how urgent), which helps prioritize cases for human review. On Claude Fable 5, it catches 78% of potentially harmful conversations flagged by a stronger classifier, and 94% of high-priority ones, at a 1% false-positive rate. It helped uncover 100K+ child-abuse flags from a single API customer, reported to authorities, plus an automated romance-scam operation run through Claude Code. Anthropic admits it’s weak as a lone blocker, cutting attack success in red-team tests only from 79% to 54%, though it made each successful attack cost ~4x more. Why it matters: After Anthropic’s own reports showed Claude being misused for cyberattacks and weapons work, letting the AI check and flag misuse in its own chats is a welcome layer. Claude brings everything it understands to each judgment, but it can also share the same blind spots, meaning the system isn’t foolproof (yet!). QUICK HITS COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY ▸ Michael used Claude Cowork to build a 3D home design app Today’s workflow comes from reader Michael Saif : “I built this web app for a friend who is building a house. It lets you see the finished version of every room in the planned home before anything is built. I described the idea to Claude Cowork, had a short back-and-forth answering its questions, and it built the app in four stages. You can upload one or more floor plans, select a room, and view it from several rotatable 3D angles. You can then describe how you want the room to look when completed, such as ‘Show me with a dark-colored wood floor with blue walls,’ and ask for changes, like light-colored wood floors. You can also add furniture to see how the room will look when finished, save multiple designs for each room, and export any image as a PNG. The whole build took less than an hour from start to finish.” See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub → How do you use AI?   • Officials didn’t believe Jensen knew of her alleged role when Trump was briefed; he never got a defensive briefing, often given to U.S. citizens targeted by spies.

  • Megaspeed, already under U.S. probe for steering Nvidia chips to China, bought at least $4.8B in Nvidia gear via a sister firm, and remains an Nvidia cloud partner.

  • Nvidia called Jensen’s meetings with Ms. Huang routine, saying customers get ordinary business info and “zero information relevant to national security.”

  • Megaspeed said outside counsel is investigating and it’s cooperating with the U.S., while China called the claims “groundless smears and slanders.”

Why it matters: The report reads like a spy thriller, but nothing has been publicly proven, including whether Ms. Huang passed anything to China. The immediate fallout may hit the loophole allowing firms like Megaspeed to rent Nvidia-powered computing from Southeast Asia to Chinese AI labs — one Trump reopened but may now close.

TOGETHER WITH OPENART🧑‍🎨 Create a launch video for your business 

The Rundown: Need a launch video for your business? Simply paste your website link, add your brand assets, and define your target audience. OpenArt’s AI video agent will shape the story and messaging while handling the script, motion design, voiceover, and video editing.

With OpenArt, you can:

  • Turn your website, screenshots, or pitch deck into a launch video

  • Create short promos or longer videos to showcase your business

  • Refine scenes, voiceovers, or music by describing the changes

  • Go beyond launches with product ads and UGC-style videos

Create your launch video with OpenArt.

ROWAN’S CORNER🤖 ‘Sent from my agent’

h/t to @gregisenberg for the tweet

Rowan: “Sent from my agent” is becoming the new “Sent from iPhone.” That’s a tweet my friend Greg Isenberg recently made that’s stirring up conversation.

Basically, “Sent from my iPhone” started as a way to buy forgiveness for typos and messy formatting when emailing someone from your iPhone. But when someone sees “Sent from my agent,” the real message they receive is: you weren’t worth my attention.

There’s real tension here (for me included). Agents are the biggest leverage available right now, and I run several tasks through them, saving me at least a few hours a week. But I also believe going the extra mile and writing something yourself shows the other human respect.

So here’s my line:

  1. Anything that touches a person is me — social posts, messages, recruiting calls, live video.

  2. Anything that’s a task, an agent can do.

I also have a growing thesis that real human relationships will only become more valuable as AI gets better. Anything that risks that trust is probably a bad trade. Personally, if I see “sent from my agent,” I’m deleting the email.

I’ve written before that AI intuition is the most important skill of this decade, knowing which tasks to hand to AI, and this is the perfect example. Use agents everywhere, except on people.

Are you using agents to respond to your emails, or do you think the human touch shows respect? Let me know in the poll at the bottom of the email. I’m curious!

AI TRAINING🎙️ Make ElevenLabs voiceovers sound more natural

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll add Audio Tags to a short Eleven v4 voiceover, compare it with the plain version, and create a short scene with two speakers.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open ElevenLabs Text to Speech, choose one voice, and select Eleven v4. Generate the guide’s plain script and save it for comparison

  2. Paste the tagged version without changing the spoken words. Keep the same voice and settings so you can hear the difference

  3. Compare the opening, pace, and final line. If the delivery stays flat, make one cue more specific. Change one thing at a time

  4. If a tag gets read aloud, check the model and square brackets. Keep the direction short and place it before the words it should affect

  5. Open Dialogue mode, add two voices, and generate the guide’s exchange. Check the words, speakers, and timing before downloading the clips

Pro tip: Save a plain version before adding tags. A more expressive read may still sound less natural. You can find our full cheat sheet, annotated scripts, and review checklist here.

PRESENTED BY GLEAN🚀 From data to decisions, faster

The Rundown: Business data spans across apps, warehouses, and BI platforms, while the context behind the numbers lives in documents, tickets, and conversations. Glean’s upcoming webinar helps you bring it all together, find trusted answers, and make data-driven decisions without SQL or a BI background.

In this webinar, you’ll learn how to:

  • Query business data in natural language

  • Connect metrics with enterprise context

Register for the webinar and put AI to work.

ANTHROPIC / AI SAFETY🚨 Anthropic’s AI now monitors its own conversations

Image source: Anthropic

The Rundown: Anthropic introduced “self-assessment,” a technique where Claude reviews the chat after each reply and flags potential misuse, saying the system has been active since June and catching large-scale abuse that might otherwise be missed.

The details:

  • Claude gives each conversation a quick safety verdict (whether it’s harmful, what kind of harm, and how urgent), which helps prioritize cases for human review.

  • On Claude Fable 5, it catches 78% of potentially harmful conversations flagged by a stronger classifier, and 94% of high-priority ones, at a 1% false-positive rate.

  • It helped uncover 100K+ child-abuse flags from a single API customer, reported to authorities, plus an automated romance-scam operation run through Claude Code.

  • Anthropic admits it’s weak as a lone blocker, cutting attack success in red-team tests only from 79% to 54%, though it made each successful attack cost ~4x more.

Why it matters: After Anthropic’s own reports showed Claude being misused for cyberattacks and weapons work, letting the AI check and flag misuse in its own chats is a welcome layer. Claude brings everything it understands to each judgment, but it can also share the same blind spots, meaning the system isn’t foolproof (yet!).

items.title: Why Self-Hosted GLM-5.3 Needs 8 GPUs, Not 4, for Long Coding Sessions
items.summary:
​ Revolut’s David Abitbol says GLM-5.3 fits on 4 GPUs but runs short of memory. The reason is in vLLM’s source: every GPU keeps a full copy of each chat’s memory, the KV cache. If you self-host GLM-5.3 with vLLM for long coding sessions, give each copy of the model 8 B200 GPUs, not 4, even though it fits on 4. On paper, 4 GPUs leave room for 3.0 full 256K-token sessions per copy; 8 GPUs leave room for 7.6. This article shows why and gives you a 69-line script to check your own setup before you rent anything. 01 — Where this comes from On October 29 the AI Engineer YouTube channel posted “How Revolut Cut AI Coding Costs 90% With Self-Hosted Open Models” , a 12-minute talk by David Abitbol of Revolut. Paraphrasing his points from the auto-generated captions: serving about 2,000 engineers takes roughly 56 B200s for GLM-5.3. Keep time to first token under 3 seconds. Long context is a scam; 256K is what you need. Use NVFP4 on Blackwell GPUs, about 40% smaller than FP8. And although GLM fits on 4 GPUs (TP4), you don’t get enough KV cache, so 8 (TP8) may work better. He gave the rules but not the math. Here it is. 02 — The short answer: the memory is copied The KV cache is the model’s memory of each conversation. GLM-5.3 uses DeepSeek-style latent attention, which stores a small cache per token. When you split a model across 4 GPUs (tensor parallelism), the weights get split. In vLLM 0.32.0 this cache does not. The attention layer declares its cache with max_tp_shards=1, and the field's docstring in kv_cache_interface.py says GPUs beyond that "hold replicas". So each GPU keeps a full copy of every conversation's cache. Going from 4 GPUs to 8 halves the weights on each GPU. All the memory that frees up becomes cache. 03 — How big is the cache per token? Two numbers come from the vLLM 0.32.0 source: 576 bytes per token per layer for the main cache. The NVFP4 checkpoint declares an 8-bit float KV cache (and vLLM also defaults GLM-5.3 to fp8 on B200s). For an fp8 cache, vLLM’s backend list puts FlashInfer’s sparse kernel first, and it stores 576 one-byte values. 132 bytes per token for the sparse-attention “indexer” cache, which only some layers have. vLLM builds an indexer on a layer when max(layer - offset + 1, 0) % freq == 0. With GLM-5.3's freq of 4 and offset of 3, that's 21 of 78 layers. The config's own indexer_types list also marks 21 layers as full. 04 — The script​ glmfit.py reads the model's config.json and model.safetensors.index.json. It uses only Python's standard library and needs no GPU. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """How much KV cache does GLM-5.3 get on B200s at TP4 vs TP8? usage: glmfit.py config.json model.safetensors.index.json [other.index.json] Byte constants are read from vLLM 0.32.0 source (see comments).""" import json, os, sys # MLA row: 576 = fp8_e4m3, FlashInfer sparse (B200 default for an fp8 cache) # 656 = fp8_ds_mla, --attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE IDX = 128 + 128 // 128 * 4 # Indexer k_cache: head_dim + scales env = os.environ.get MLA = int(env("MLA", 576)) HBM, UTIL = float(env("HBM_GB", 180)), float(env("UTIL", 0.92)) OVH, GPUS = float(env("OVERHEAD_GB", 12)), int(env("GPUS", 56)) CTX, MTP = int(env("CTX", 262144)), int(env("MTP", 0)) DCP = int(env("DCP", 1)) # vLLM -dcp; 1 = off def load(p): try: return json.load(open(p)) except (OSError, ValueError) as e: sys.exit(f"usage: glmfit.py config.json index.json [index2]
{e}") def indexer_layers(c): # vLLM models/deepseek_v32/attention.py: Indexer unless skip_topk f, off = c.get("index_topk_freq", 1), c.get("index_skip_topk_offset", 2) pat = c.get("index_topk_pattern") n = c["num_hidden_layers"] if pat: return sum(pat[i] != "S" for i in range(n)) return sum(max(i - off + 1, 0) % f == 0 for i in range(n)) if len(sys.argv) < 3: sys.exit(__doc__.splitlines()[1]) cfg, idx = load(sys.argv[1]), load(sys.argv[2]) wt = idx["metadata"]["total_size"] / 1e9 n = cfg["num_hidden_layers"] + MTP ni = indexer_layers(cfg) + MTP per_tok = MLA * n + IDX * ni sess = CTX * per_tok / 1e9 listed = sum(t == "full" for t in cfg.get("indexer_types", [])) print(f"weights {wt:7.2f} GB (index.json total_size)") print(f"indexer {ni} of {n} layers (vLLM rule; config lists {listed})") print(f"KV per token {per_tok:,} B = {MLA} x {n} MLA" f" + {IDX} x {ni} indexer") print(f"one {CTX:,}-token session = {sess:.2f} GB;" " at dcp=1 every TP rank holds all of it") print(f"budget {HBM:.0f} GB x {UTIL:.2f} - {OVH:.0f} GB overhead" " (assumed)
") full = cfg["max_position_embeddings"] * per_tok / 1e9 print("TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU tok/replica sess reps fleet tok 1M?") for tp in (4, 8): w = wt / tp # even split: approximation kv = HBM * UTIL - OVH - w reps = GPUS // tp if kv <= 0: print(f"{tp:<2} {'-':>3} {w:6.2f} weights alone exceed the budget") continue d = DCP if tp % DCP == 0 else 1 # vLLM refuses tp % dcp != 0 tok = kv * 1e9 * d / per_tok # dcp=1: every rank holds a full copy boot = "boots" if kv * d >= full else "no" print(f"{tp:<2} {d:3} {w:6.2f} {kv:6.2f} {tok:11,.0f} {tok / CTX:5.2f}" f" {reps:4} {tok * reps / 1e6:8.2f}M {boot}") print(f"
1M? = can vLLM start with max_model_len" f" {cfg['max_position_embeddings']:,} ({full:.2f} GB)") if len(sys.argv) > 3: o = load(sys.argv[3])["metadata"]["total_size"] / 1e9 print(f"other checkpoint {o:.2f} GB; this one is" f" {100 * (1 - wt / o):.1f}% smaller") ​ 05 — Run it From nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4, download config.json and model.safetensors.index.json (save it as nvfp4.index.json). From zai-org/GLM-5.3, the FP8 release, download the index too (save it as fp8.index.json). Then: python3 glmfit.py config.json nvfp4.index.json fp8.index.json weights 464.12 GB (index.json total_size) indexer 21 of 78 layers (vLLM rule; config lists 21) KV per token 47,700 B = 576 x 78 MLA + 132 x 21 indexer one 262,144-token session = 12.50 GB; at dcp=1 every TP rank holds all of it budget 180 GB x 0.92 - 12 GB overhead (assumed) TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU tok/replica sess reps fleet tok 1M? 4 1 116.03 37.57 787,653 3.00 14 11.03M no 8 1 58.01 95.59 2,003,889 7.64 7 14.03M boots 1M? = can vLLM start with max_model_len 1,048,576 (50.02 GB) other checkpoint 755.62 GB; this one is 38.6% smaller Read the sess column: full 256K sessions per copy of the model. TP4 gets 3.00 and TP8 gets 7.64. Across 56 GPUs, TP4's 14 copies hold 11.03M cached tokens and TP8's 7 copies hold 14.03M. That's 27% more cache from half as many copies. 06 — Is NVFP4 really 40% smaller? The last line compares the two checkpoints’ total_size: 464.12 GB for NVIDIA's NVFP4 against 755.62 GB for Z.ai's FP8. That's 38.6% smaller, close to the talk's "about 40%". Why not 50%, if 4 bits is half of 8? The Hub lists 27.9 billion BF16 parameters in the NVFP4 repo. Its config puts only the mlp.experts modules in NVFP4 and the first three dense MLPs in FP8. The multi-token-prediction layer, model.layers.78*, is excluded from quantization. The rest stays BF16. 07 — Why 1M context won’t start on 4 GPUs by default GLM-5.3’s config advertises max_position_embeddings: 1048576. vLLM's check_enough_kv_cache_memory refuses to start if a single request of max_model_len can't fit. At 47,700 bytes a token, one 1M-token request needs 50.02 GB. On TP4 each GPU has 37.57 GB for cache, and each GPU must hold the whole request. So the 1M? column says no. Set --max-model-len to 256K (anything under about 787K tokens fits) and, by the script's numbers, the startup check passes. "Long context is a scam" is literally true here. 08 — The FP8 version doesn’t fit on 4 GPUs at all python3 glmfit.py config.json fp8.index.json ​ TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU tok/replica sess reps fleet tok 1M? 4 - 188.90 weights alone exceed the budget 8 1 94.45 59.15 1,239,997 4.73 7 8.68M boots Same config.json; only the weight size changes. At 188.90 GB per GPU, FP8 weights alone are bigger than the 153.6 GB the script leaves for weights and cache. On 8 GPUs it fits but holds 4.73 sessions against NVFP4's 7.64. NVFP4 is what makes 4 GPUs possible at all. 09 — Two settings worth trying First, vLLM can split the cache across GPUs instead of copying it: --decode-context-parallel-size (-dcp). When vLLM checks whether a max-length request fits, it divides max_model_len by the DCP size. The script assumes the cache splits evenly. With DCP=8: TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU tok/replica sess reps fleet tok 1M? 4 1 116.03 37.57 787,653 3.00 14 11.03M no 8 8 58.01 95.59 16,031,116 61.15 7 112.22M boots TP8 goes from 7.64 to 61.15 sessions per copy. vLLM refuses -dcp 8 on 4 GPUs (the GPU count must be divisible by the DCP size), so the script shows that row with DCP off. With DCP=4, TP4 reaches 12.02 sessions and TP8 30.58, so 8 GPUs still hold more. I read this in source and did not run it on B200s. DCP adds GPU-to-GPU traffic on every decode step, so measure speed before you trust it. The default FlashInfer backend supports DCP with GLM’s a2a default. If you switch to the FlashMLA backend, it only accepts --dcp-comm-backend ag_rs. Second, the FlashMLA backend (--attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE) stores 656 bytes per layer instead of 576. Run MLA=656 and the numbers drop to 2.66 and 6.76 sessions. 8 GPUs still hold over 2.5 times as many.​ 10 — What the script assumes 180 GB per B200 and vLLM’s default gpu_memory_utilization of 0.92. 12 GB per GPU for activations, CUDA graphs and communication. That’s a guess. With OVERHEAD_GB=24, TP4 drops to 2.04 sessions and TP8 to 6.68. Weights split evenly across GPUs. Real splits copy a few small tensors. No speculative-decoding layer. MTP=1 adds one cache layer and one indexer layer. vLLM’s data-parallel attention mode, which also avoids the copy, isn’t modelled. Every session, token, GB and percentage in sections 05–10 comes from glmfit.py, either in the output blocks or from the env runs named beside them (DCP=8, DCP=4, MLA=656, OVERHEAD_GB=24, MTP=1). The 27% and 153.6 GB are arithmetic on its output, and the lede rounds 3.00 and 7.64. The talk's figures (56 B200s, 2,000 engineers, 3 seconds, about 40%) come from the captions. The Hub's dtype counts and quantization layout in section 06, and the vLLM file references, come from the Hub pages and the vLLM 0.32.0 wheel. None of this was run on a GPU. 11 — Verdict vLLM keeps a full copy of GLM-5.3’s attention cache on every GPU in a tensor-parallel group. On paper that gives 8 GPUs 7.64 full 256K sessions per copy against 3.00 for 4 GPUs, and without DCP, 4 GPUs can’t even start at the advertised 1M context. Revolut’s advice, to cap context at 256K and try 8 GPUs, matches what vLLM’s code implies. When you size a self-hosted coding model, do you count the weights, or the sessions the cache can hold? If this saved you a GPU order, a clap helps others find it. Follow me for daily LLM deep-dives. Why Self-Hosted GLM-5.3 Needs 8 GPUs, Not 4, for Long Coding Sessions was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
​

Revolut’s David Abitbol says GLM-5.3 fits on 4 GPUs but runs short of memory. The reason is in vLLM’s source: every GPU keeps a full copy of each chat’s memory, the KV cache.

If you self-host GLM-5.3 with vLLM for long coding sessions, give each copy of the model 8 B200 GPUs, not 4, even though it fits on 4. On paper, 4 GPUs leave room for 3.0 full 256K-token sessions per copy; 8 GPUs leave room for 7.6. This article shows why and gives you a 69-line script to check your own setup before you rent anything.

01 — Where this comes from

On October 29 the AI Engineer YouTube channel posted “How Revolut Cut AI Coding Costs 90% With Self-Hosted Open Models”, a 12-minute talk by David Abitbol of Revolut.

Paraphrasing his points from the auto-generated captions: serving about 2,000 engineers takes roughly 56 B200s for GLM-5.3. Keep time to first token under 3 seconds. Long context is a scam; 256K is what you need. Use NVFP4 on Blackwell GPUs, about 40% smaller than FP8. And although GLM fits on 4 GPUs (TP4), you don’t get enough KV cache, so 8 (TP8) may work better.

He gave the rules but not the math. Here it is.

02 — The short answer: the memory is copied

The KV cache is the model’s memory of each conversation. GLM-5.3 uses DeepSeek-style latent attention, which stores a small cache per token.

When you split a model across 4 GPUs (tensor parallelism), the weights get split. In vLLM 0.32.0 this cache does not. The attention layer declares its cache with max_tp_shards=1, and the field's docstring in kv_cache_interface.py says GPUs beyond that "hold replicas". So each GPU keeps a full copy of every conversation's cache.

Going from 4 GPUs to 8 halves the weights on each GPU. All the memory that frees up becomes cache.

03 — How big is the cache per token?

Two numbers come from the vLLM 0.32.0 source:

  • 576 bytes per token per layer for the main cache. The NVFP4 checkpoint declares an 8-bit float KV cache (and vLLM also defaults GLM-5.3 to fp8 on B200s). For an fp8 cache, vLLM’s backend list puts FlashInfer’s sparse kernel first, and it stores 576 one-byte values.
  • 132 bytes per token for the sparse-attention “indexer” cache, which only some layers have.

vLLM builds an indexer on a layer when max(layer - offset + 1, 0) % freq == 0. With GLM-5.3's freq of 4 and offset of 3, that's 21 of 78 layers. The config's own indexer_types list also marks 21 layers as full.

04 — The script​

glmfit.py reads the model's config.json and model.safetensors.index.json. It uses only Python's standard library and needs no GPU.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""How much KV cache does GLM-5.3 get on B200s at TP4 vs TP8?
usage: glmfit.py config.json model.safetensors.index.json [other.index.json]
Byte constants are read from vLLM 0.32.0 source (see comments)."""
import json, os, sys
# MLA row: 576 = fp8_e4m3, FlashInfer sparse (B200 default for an fp8 cache)
#          656 = fp8_ds_mla, --attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE
IDX = 128 + 128 // 128 * 4         # Indexer k_cache: head_dim + scales
env = os.environ.get
MLA = int(env("MLA", 576))
HBM, UTIL = float(env("HBM_GB", 180)), float(env("UTIL", 0.92))
OVH, GPUS = float(env("OVERHEAD_GB", 12)), int(env("GPUS", 56))
CTX, MTP = int(env("CTX", 262144)), int(env("MTP", 0))
DCP = int(env("DCP", 1))            # vLLM -dcp; 1 = off
def load(p):
    try:
        return json.load(open(p))
    except (OSError, ValueError) as e:
        sys.exit(f"usage: glmfit.py config.json index.json [index2]
{e}")
def indexer_layers(c):
    # vLLM models/deepseek_v32/attention.py: Indexer unless skip_topk
    f, off = c.get("index_topk_freq", 1), c.get("index_skip_topk_offset", 2)
    pat = c.get("index_topk_pattern")
    n = c["num_hidden_layers"]
    if pat:
        return sum(pat[i] != "S" for i in range(n))
    return sum(max(i - off + 1, 0) % f == 0 for i in range(n))
if len(sys.argv) < 3:
    sys.exit(__doc__.splitlines()[1])
cfg, idx = load(sys.argv[1]), load(sys.argv[2])
wt = idx["metadata"]["total_size"] / 1e9
n = cfg["num_hidden_layers"] + MTP
ni = indexer_layers(cfg) + MTP
per_tok = MLA * n + IDX * ni
sess = CTX * per_tok / 1e9
listed = sum(t == "full" for t in cfg.get("indexer_types", []))
print(f"weights      {wt:7.2f} GB  (index.json total_size)")
print(f"indexer      {ni} of {n} layers (vLLM rule; config lists {listed})")
print(f"KV per token {per_tok:,} B = {MLA} x {n} MLA"
      f" + {IDX} x {ni} indexer")
print(f"one {CTX:,}-token session = {sess:.2f} GB;"
      " at dcp=1 every TP rank holds all of it")
print(f"budget       {HBM:.0f} GB x {UTIL:.2f} - {OVH:.0f} GB overhead"
      " (assumed)
")
full = cfg["max_position_embeddings"] * per_tok / 1e9
print("TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU  tok/replica  sess reps  fleet tok  1M?")
for tp in (4, 8):
    w = wt / tp                      # even split: approximation
    kv = HBM * UTIL - OVH - w
    reps = GPUS // tp
    if kv <= 0:
        print(f"{tp:<2} {'-':>3} {w:6.2f}  weights alone exceed the budget")
        continue
    d = DCP if tp % DCP == 0 else 1  # vLLM refuses tp % dcp != 0
    tok = kv * 1e9 * d / per_tok     # dcp=1: every rank holds a full copy
    boot = "boots" if kv * d >= full else "no"
    print(f"{tp:<2} {d:3} {w:6.2f} {kv:6.2f}  {tok:11,.0f} {tok / CTX:5.2f}"
          f" {reps:4} {tok * reps / 1e6:8.2f}M  {boot}")
print(f"
1M? = can vLLM start with max_model_len"
      f" {cfg['max_position_embeddings']:,} ({full:.2f} GB)")
if len(sys.argv) > 3:
    o = load(sys.argv[3])["metadata"]["total_size"] / 1e9
    print(f"other checkpoint {o:.2f} GB; this one is"
          f" {100 * (1 - wt / o):.1f}% smaller")

​

05 — Run it

From nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4, download config.json and model.safetensors.index.json (save it as nvfp4.index.json). From zai-org/GLM-5.3, the FP8 release, download the index too (save it as fp8.index.json). Then:

python3 glmfit.py config.json nvfp4.index.json fp8.index.json
weights       464.12 GB  (index.json total_size)
indexer      21 of 78 layers (vLLM rule; config lists 21)
KV per token 47,700 B = 576 x 78 MLA + 132 x 21 indexer
one 262,144-token session = 12.50 GB; at dcp=1 every TP rank holds all of it
budget       180 GB x 0.92 - 12 GB overhead (assumed)
TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU  tok/replica  sess reps  fleet tok  1M?
4    1 116.03  37.57      787,653  3.00   14    11.03M  no
8    1  58.01  95.59    2,003,889  7.64    7    14.03M  boots
1M? = can vLLM start with max_model_len 1,048,576 (50.02 GB)
other checkpoint 755.62 GB; this one is 38.6% smaller

Read the sess column: full 256K sessions per copy of the model. TP4 gets 3.00 and TP8 gets 7.64. Across 56 GPUs, TP4's 14 copies hold 11.03M cached tokens and TP8's 7 copies hold 14.03M. That's 27% more cache from half as many copies.

06 — Is NVFP4 really 40% smaller?

The last line compares the two checkpoints’ total_size: 464.12 GB for NVIDIA's NVFP4 against 755.62 GB for Z.ai's FP8. That's 38.6% smaller, close to the talk's "about 40%".

Why not 50%, if 4 bits is half of 8? The Hub lists 27.9 billion BF16 parameters in the NVFP4 repo. Its config puts only the mlp.experts modules in NVFP4 and the first three dense MLPs in FP8. The multi-token-prediction layer, model.layers.78*, is excluded from quantization. The rest stays BF16.

07 — Why 1M context won’t start on 4 GPUs by default

GLM-5.3’s config advertises max_position_embeddings: 1048576. vLLM's check_enough_kv_cache_memory refuses to start if a single request of max_model_len can't fit. At 47,700 bytes a token, one 1M-token request needs 50.02 GB.

On TP4 each GPU has 37.57 GB for cache, and each GPU must hold the whole request. So the 1M? column says no. Set --max-model-len to 256K (anything under about 787K tokens fits) and, by the script's numbers, the startup check passes. "Long context is a scam" is literally true here.

08 — The FP8 version doesn’t fit on 4 GPUs at all
python3 glmfit.py config.json fp8.index.json

​

TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU  tok/replica  sess reps  fleet tok  1M?
4    - 188.90  weights alone exceed the budget
8    1  94.45  59.15    1,239,997  4.73    7     8.68M  boots

Same config.json; only the weight size changes. At 188.90 GB per GPU, FP8 weights alone are bigger than the 153.6 GB the script leaves for weights and cache. On 8 GPUs it fits but holds 4.73 sessions against NVFP4's 7.64. NVFP4 is what makes 4 GPUs possible at all.

09 — Two settings worth trying

First, vLLM can split the cache across GPUs instead of copying it: --decode-context-parallel-size (-dcp). When vLLM checks whether a max-length request fits, it divides max_model_len by the DCP size. The script assumes the cache splits evenly. With DCP=8:

TP dcp wt/GPU KV/GPU  tok/replica  sess reps  fleet tok  1M?
4    1 116.03  37.57      787,653  3.00   14    11.03M  no
8    8  58.01  95.59   16,031,116 61.15    7   112.22M  boots

TP8 goes from 7.64 to 61.15 sessions per copy. vLLM refuses -dcp 8 on 4 GPUs (the GPU count must be divisible by the DCP size), so the script shows that row with DCP off. With DCP=4, TP4 reaches 12.02 sessions and TP8 30.58, so 8 GPUs still hold more.

I read this in source and did not run it on B200s. DCP adds GPU-to-GPU traffic on every decode step, so measure speed before you trust it. The default FlashInfer backend supports DCP with GLM’s a2a default. If you switch to the FlashMLA backend, it only accepts --dcp-comm-backend ag_rs.

Second, the FlashMLA backend (--attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE) stores 656 bytes per layer instead of 576. Run MLA=656 and the numbers drop to 2.66 and 6.76 sessions. 8 GPUs still hold over 2.5 times as many.​

10 — What the script assumes
  • 180 GB per B200 and vLLM’s default gpu_memory_utilization of 0.92.
  • 12 GB per GPU for activations, CUDA graphs and communication. That’s a guess. With OVERHEAD_GB=24, TP4 drops to 2.04 sessions and TP8 to 6.68.
  • Weights split evenly across GPUs. Real splits copy a few small tensors.
  • No speculative-decoding layer. MTP=1 adds one cache layer and one indexer layer.
  • vLLM’s data-parallel attention mode, which also avoids the copy, isn’t modelled.

Every session, token, GB and percentage in sections 05–10 comes from glmfit.py, either in the output blocks or from the env runs named beside them (DCP=8, DCP=4, MLA=656, OVERHEAD_GB=24, MTP=1). The 27% and 153.6 GB are arithmetic on its output, and the lede rounds 3.00 and 7.64. The talk's figures (56 B200s, 2,000 engineers, 3 seconds, about 40%) come from the captions. The Hub's dtype counts and quantization layout in section 06, and the vLLM file references, come from the Hub pages and the vLLM 0.32.0 wheel. None of this was run on a GPU.

11 — Verdict

vLLM keeps a full copy of GLM-5.3’s attention cache on every GPU in a tensor-parallel group. On paper that gives 8 GPUs 7.64 full 256K sessions per copy against 3.00 for 4 GPUs, and without DCP, 4 GPUs can’t even start at the advertised 1M context. Revolut’s advice, to cap context at 256K and try 8 GPUs, matches what vLLM’s code implies.

When you size a self-hosted coding model, do you count the weights, or the sessions the cache can hold?

If this saved you a GPU order, a clap helps others find it.

Follow me for daily LLM deep-dives.
