items.title: Moving a production API to Hetzner, part 1: choosing and creating the server
items.summary: Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over I recently moved a small production API from one VPS provider to Hetzner Cloud. The stack is ordinary: a Rust web server, PostgreSQL, Valkey (the open-source Redis fork), and Caddy as the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, all under Docker Compose. Encrypted blobs live in S3-compatible object storage, which doesn't move at all. These posts are both the record of what I did and a tutorial. Each step comes with the command , what it does , and why it works that way , because most migration guides give the commands and skip the reasons, and the reasons are what you need when something goes wrong. Plenty did go wrong, and I've left those parts in. Throughout, the addresses are placeholders from the documentation ranges reserved for examples (RFC 5737 and RFC 3849): Placeholder Means 203.0.113.10 the old server 198.51.100.20 the new Hetzner server 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 the new server's IPv6 range api.example.com the API's domain old-box , new-box SSH aliases for the two servers (set up in part 2) What we are moving Only Caddy publishes ports to the outside world. Everything else talks over Docker's private network. That detail comes back several times, because it decides what the firewall has to allow and what the migration has to copy. 1. Picking a server type The three families When you click Add Server , the Type step splits the catalogue into Shared Resources (two families) and Dedicated Resources (one): Family Series CPU Hetzner's own pitch Who it's for Cost-Optimized (shared) CX (x86) and CAX (Arm64) shared Intel/AMD, older hardware generations "cost-efficient… with limited availability" small production services, side projects. Cheapest per GB of RAM Regular Performance (shared) CPX shared AMD, newer hardware generations "best price/performance" the same jobs with faster, more consistent CPU General Purpose (dedicated) CCX dedicated AMD vCPUs, latest hardware "predictable performance, critical production" sustained CPU load: builds, busy databases Here is each family as the console showed it in Helsinki on the day I created the server (October 2026, USD per month, excluding VAT): Cost-Optimized. CX23 is 2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB for $6.49. Note that every row is greyed out : at that moment none of them could be ordered in Helsinki. The summary on the right still says CPX22 because a greyed row can't be selected. Regular Performance. CPX22 has the same 2 vCPU and 4 GB as CX23 (with 80 GB of disk) for $22.99, more than three times the price. General Purpose. Dedicated cores start at CCX13 (2 vCPU, 8 GB) for $50.49. The panel on the right shows one cost that's easy to miss: a public IPv4 is billed on top of the server, $0.60/month. Cost-Optimized also offers Arm64 (Ampere) , which is often the best value of all. I couldn't use it: our container image is built for amd64 only. Check your image's architecture before choosing Arm. docker manifest inspect lists the platforms it was built for. "Shared" means your virtual CPU is a time slice of a physical core that other customers' VMs use too. Most of the time you get the whole slice. When a neighbour is busy you may get less, which is called CPU steal (shown as st in top ). For an API that idles most of the day that's fine; for a CI runner, it isn't. Dedicated vCPUs are reserved for you, which is what the large price jump buys. How big does it have to be? Measure before you buy. On the old server, docker stats --no-stream and free -h showed the entire stack using about 1 GB. On the fresh Hetzner box, Ubuntu itself sat at about 500 MB used after boot. Option (Helsinki, October 2026) vCPU / RAM / disk Monthly + IPv4 Verdict CPX02 (Regular Performance) 1 / 1 GB / 20 GB $7.49 + $0.60 too small : Postgres, Valkey, the server and Caddy together would spill into swap CPX12 (Regular Performance) 1 / 2 GB / 40 GB $13.49 + $0.60 tight on RAM, and double CX23's price CX23 (Cost-Optimized) 2 / 4 GB / 40 GB $6.49 + $0.60 chosen : 4× headroom on RAM, the cheapest option that fits CPX22 (Regular Performance) 2 / 4 GB / 80 GB $22.99 + $0.60 the fallback if CX23 stays unavailable CCX13 (General Purpose) 2 dedicated / 8 GB / 80 GB $50.49 + $0.60 far more than an idle API needs Prices change; take today's from the console, not from this table. "Limited availability" is real Cost-Optimized types carry a limited availability label, and it means it. When I first configured the server, CX23 in Helsinki was available. A few minutes later, when I came back to click Create, the whole CX row set was greyed out: not available (the first screenshot above).. Hetzner allocates these types from a pool of hosts per location. When a location's pool is full, the type disappears there until capacity frees up. Your options: Change the location. Nuremberg ( nbg1 ) and Falkenstein ( fsn1 ) in Germany and Helsinki ( hel1 ) in Finland are all in the eu-central network zone, with similar latency to most of Europe. The type is often in stock at one of the others. Wait and retry. Capacity comes and goes during the day. My CX23 in Helsinki came back later. Pick the next family up (CPX), if you can't wait and the price is acceptable. A consequence I didn't expect: once you hold a scarce server type, deleting the server to fix a mistake is risky. You may not get another one. That shaped part 2, where I fixed a setup mistake on the running server instead of recreating it. Location and image Location : as close as possible to your users and to your object storage. My storage is a global-anycast S3 provider, so any EU location was fine. Image : Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. "LTS" means five years of security updates, which is what you want on a server you'd rather not rebuild. 24.04 LTS would have been equally good. 2. SSH keys: how you'll get in What a key pair is An SSH key pair is two halves of one mathematical object: the private key ( ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 ) stays on your laptop and never leaves it; the public key ( ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub ) goes on every server you want to log in to, in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . The server never learns your private key. At login it asks your SSH client to sign a value that is unique to this connection. Your client signs it with the private key, and the server checks the signature against the public key it has on file. A valid signature proves you hold the private key without the key ever crossing the network. Notice there are two key pairs in play: Key Belongs to Proves Stored where host key the server "I really am 198.51.100.20, not an impostor" server: /etc/ssh/ssh_host_* ; your laptop remembers it in ~/.ssh/known_hosts user key you "I'm allowed to log in as ubuntu " laptop: private key; server: authorized_keys The first time you connect, SSH shows the host key's fingerprint and asks whether to trust it. This is called TOFU: trust on first use . If the host key later changes, for example because you rebuilt the server, SSH refuses to connect and warns about a possible man-in-the-middle. That's correct behaviour. After a deliberate rebuild, remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R . Creating the key ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -C hetzner-api -t ed25519 : a modern elliptic-curve key. It's short (one line), fast, and has no weak-parameter choices to get wrong, unlike older RSA keys. -f : the file name. A separate key per provider means losing or rotating one doesn't touch the others. -C : a comment, just a label so you can recognise the key in authorized_keys later. It asks for a passphrase. Use one: it encrypts the private key on disk, and ssh-agent remembers it for your session, so you type it once. Print the public half and paste it into Hetzner → Security → SSH keys → Add SSH key : cat ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub When you pick this key on the create screen, Hetzner writes it into the new server's /root/.ssh/authorized_keys , and, as a side effect, does not set a root password at all . Remember that; it matters in part 2. 3. Primary IPs: an address that outlives the server What a Primary IP is In Hetzner Cloud, a server's public address is a separate resource called a Primary IP . It's created along with the server and attached to it, but it has a life of its own: IPv4 : one address, billed separately (about $0.60/month), because the world has run out of IPv4. IPv6 : a whole /64 network, free. That's 2⁶⁴ addresses; the server uses the first one by convention ( 2001:db8:1234:5678::1 ). Why "auto delete" matters Each Primary IP has an auto delete switch. On, the address is released when the server is deleted, and you'll probably never get it back. Off, the address stays in your project, unattached, ready to assign to a replacement server. Why you want it off for production: DNS points at it. A new address means a DNS change, and DNS changes take a while to reach everyone (part 3 explains TTLs). Other services may allowlist it. Object-storage tokens, database firewalls and payment-provider webhook settings sometimes filter by source IP. It's your escape hatch. If the server breaks beyond repair, you can delete it and create a new one with the same address . Turn it off in IPs → (the IPv4) → ⋯ . If the menu offers "Enable Auto Delete" , it's already off. I didn't add an IPv6 (AAAA) DNS record. The old server had none, so the migration changes as little as possible. That can come later. 4. The Cloud Firewall: the perimeter outside your VM Two places a firewall can sit A Hetzner Cloud Firewall filters traffic in Hetzner's network, before it reaches your VM . A host firewall like ufw filters it inside the VM. The difference matters because of Docker. When a container publishes a port ( ports: ["443:443"] ), Docker writes its own NAT rules that send the packet to the container before it reaches the chain ufw controls. So ufw deny 443 does not block a published Docker port, and plenty of people have exposed a database to the internet this way while ufw status said everything was closed. The Cloud Firewall can't be bypassed from inside the VM, so it is the real perimeter . ufw (set up in part 2) is a second layer for anything that isn't Docker. Stateful filtering, in one paragraph Both firewalls are stateful : they track connections. You write rules for new incoming connections only. Replies to connections your server opened (to download packages, call an API, fetch a certificate) are recognised as part of an existing connection and let back in automatically. That's why the rule set below has no outbound rules at all: with no outbound rules, Hetzner allows all outbound traffic , and the server needs outbound access to apt, the container registry, object storage, the email provider and Let's Encrypt. The rules Create it before the server ( Firewalls → Create Firewall ) so the server is born protected: Protocol Port Source Why TCP 2222 Any IPv4, Any IPv6 SSH, on a non-standard port TCP 22 Any SSH, for networks that block outbound 2222 TCP 80 Any Let's Encrypt's HTTP-01 challenge, and the HTTP→HTTPS redirect TCP 443 Any the API UDP 443 Any HTTP/3 (QUIC runs over UDP) ICMP — Any ping, and path-MTU discovery (blocking all ICMP can silently break large packets) Not on the list: 5432 (Postgres) and 6379 (Valkey). They're never published, and if a misconfiguration ever did publish them, this firewall would still drop the traffic. Why two SSH ports? Port 22 gets a constant stream of automated password-guessing bots. Moving SSH to 2222 isn't security, since a port scan finds it in seconds, but it cuts that noise to almost nothing and keeps the logs readable. Key-only login (part 2) is the actual security. I kept 22 as well, because some networks block outbound connections to unusual ports. As part 2 shows, my home network turned out to do the reverse. 5. cloud-init: configuring the server before you first log in What it is cloud-init is a program in every major cloud image that runs once, on first boot . It reads "user data" the provider hands to the VM, which is the text you paste into the Cloud config box on the create screen, and applies it: creating users, writing files, installing packages, running commands. The appeal is that the server is configured before anyone logs in. You never have a window where it's reachable with default settings, and the configuration is a document you can review and reuse. #cloud-config users : - name : ubuntu groups : [ sudo ] shell : /bin/bash sudo : " ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" ssh_authorized_keys : - ssh-ed25519 AAAA...your-public-key... hetzner-api disable_root : true ssh_pwauth : false package_update : true package_upgrade : true packages : [ ufw , unattended-upgrades ] write_files : - path : /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf content : | Port 22 Port 2222 PasswordAuthentication no KbdInteractiveAuthentication no PermitRootLogin no PubkeyAuthentication yes - path : /etc/docker/daemon.json content : | {"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}} runcmd : - ufw default deny incoming - ufw default allow outgoing - ufw allow 22/tcp - ufw allow 2222/tcp - ufw allow 80/tcp - ufw allow 443/tcp - ufw allow 443/udp - ufw --force enable - systemctl daemon-reload - systemctl restart ssh.socket || true - systemctl restart ssh || true - fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile - echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' >> /etc/fstab Every line here is explained in part 2, where we apply the same settings by hand. The order cloud-init works in One thing that will surprise you if you SSH in too early: cloud-init runs its stages in order, and package_upgrade comes before runcmd . On a fresh image the upgrade can take a few minutes, and during that time port 2222 isn't open yet. cloud-init status --wait blocks until everything has finished. What actually happened I created the server with the type, location, image, SSH key and firewall all set, and forgot to paste the cloud config . The box came up as a stock image: only root , only port 22, no ubuntu user, no ufw, no swap. My first ssh -p 2222 got Connection refused . "Refused" is useful information. It means the packet reached the machine (the Cloud Firewall allowed it) and the kernel answered "nothing is listening here". A firewall drop would have shown up as a timeout instead. Part 2 goes into that difference. Since CX23 was close to sold out, I didn't delete and recreate. I applied the same configuration by hand, as root over port 22. That's part 2. 6. Create The final create screen, for reference: Field Value Location Helsinki (or wherever the type is in stock) Image Ubuntu 26.04 LTS Type Shared vCPU → Cost-Optimized → x86 → CX23 Networking Public IPv4 ✅, Public IPv6 ✅ SSH keys hetzner-api Firewalls the firewall from section 4 Backups off (the database is backed up to object storage; see part 3) Cloud config the YAML above. Don't forget it Name something meaningful. The default ubuntu-4gb-hel1-1 tells you nothing in six months Then turn off auto delete on the new IPv4 (section 3), and check that the firewall shows "Fully applied" with one server. What we have so far a CX23 with 4 GB RAM for about $7/month including IPv4; an IPv4 address that survives the server; a perimeter firewall that allows only SSH, HTTP(S) and ICMP; a stock Ubuntu, reachable as root on port 22 only, because the cloud config was never applied. In part 2 we fix that by hand: a non-root user, key-only SSH on two ports, ufw, swap, automatic security updates and Docker. Along the way: how to configure two servers in ~/.ssh/config , how to make changes over SSH without locking yourself out, and how to tell from a port test whether a firewall or a closed port is in your way.
items.summary_html:
Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over

I recently moved a small production API from one VPS provider to Hetzner Cloud.
The stack is ordinary: a Rust web server, PostgreSQL, Valkey (the open-source
Redis fork), and Caddy as the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, all under Docker
Compose. Encrypted blobs live in S3-compatible object storage, which doesn't
move at all.

These posts are both the record of what I did and a tutorial. Each step comes
with the command, what it does, and why it works that way, because
most migration guides give the commands and skip the reasons, and the reasons
are what you need when something goes wrong. Plenty did go wrong, and I've left
those parts in.

Throughout, the addresses are placeholders from the documentation ranges reserved for examples (RFC 5737 and RFC 3849):

Placeholder Means 203.0.113.10 the old server 198.51.100.20 the new Hetzner server 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 the new server's IPv6 range api.example.com the API's domain old-box, new-box SSH aliases for the two servers (set up in part 2)
What we are moving

Only Caddy publishes ports to the outside world. Everything else talks over
Docker's private network. That detail comes back several times, because it
decides what the firewall has to allow and what the migration has to copy.

1. Picking a server type The three families

When you click Add Server, the Type step splits the catalogue into
Shared Resources (two families) and Dedicated Resources (one):

Family Series CPU Hetzner's own pitch Who it's for Cost-Optimized (shared) CX (x86) and CAX (Arm64) shared Intel/AMD, older hardware generations "cost-efficient… with limited availability" small production services, side projects. Cheapest per GB of RAM Regular Performance (shared) CPX shared AMD, newer hardware generations "best price/performance" the same jobs with faster, more consistent CPU General Purpose (dedicated) CCX dedicated AMD vCPUs, latest hardware "predictable performance, critical production" sustained CPU load: builds, busy databases

Here is each family as the console showed it in Helsinki on the day I
created the server (October 2026, USD per month, excluding VAT):

Cost-Optimized. CX23 is 2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB for $6.49. Note that every row is greyed out: at that moment none of them could be ordered in Helsinki. The
summary on the right still says CPX22 because a greyed row can't be selected.

Regular Performance. CPX22 has the same 2 vCPU and 4 GB as CX23 (with 80 GB of disk) for $22.99, more than three times the price.

General Purpose. Dedicated cores start at CCX13 (2 vCPU, 8 GB) for $50.49.

The panel on the right shows one cost that's easy to miss: a public IPv4 is billed on top of the server, $0.60/month.

Cost-Optimized also offers Arm64 (Ampere), which is often the best value of all. I couldn't use it: our container image is built for amd64 only.

Check your image's architecture before choosing Arm. docker manifest inspect lists the platforms it was built for.

"Shared" means your virtual CPU is a time slice of a physical core that other
customers' VMs use too. Most of the time you get the whole slice. When a
neighbour is busy you may get less, which is called CPU steal (shown as st
in top). For an API that idles most of the day that's fine; for a CI runner,
it isn't. Dedicated vCPUs are reserved for you, which is what the large price
jump buys.

How big does it have to be?

Measure before you buy. On the old server, docker stats --no-stream and
free -h showed the entire stack using about 1 GB. On the fresh Hetzner box,
Ubuntu itself sat at about 500 MB used after boot.

Option (Helsinki, October 2026) vCPU / RAM / disk Monthly + IPv4 Verdict CPX02 (Regular Performance) 1 / 1 GB / 20 GB $7.49 + $0.60 too small: Postgres, Valkey, the server and Caddy together would spill into swap CPX12 (Regular Performance) 1 / 2 GB / 40 GB $13.49 + $0.60 tight on RAM, and double CX23's price CX23 (Cost-Optimized) 2 / 4 GB / 40 GB $6.49 + $0.60 chosen: 4× headroom on RAM, the cheapest option that fits CPX22 (Regular Performance) 2 / 4 GB / 80 GB $22.99 + $0.60 the fallback if CX23 stays unavailable CCX13 (General Purpose) 2 dedicated / 8 GB / 80 GB $50.49 + $0.60 far more than an idle API needs

Prices change; take today's from the console, not from this table.

"Limited availability" is real

Cost-Optimized types carry a limited availability label, and it means it. When
I first configured the server, CX23 in Helsinki was available. A few minutes later,
when I came back to click Create, the whole CX row set was greyed out: not available (the first screenshot above)..

Hetzner allocates these types from a pool of hosts per location. When a
location's pool is full, the type disappears there until capacity frees up.
Your options:

  1. Change the location. Nuremberg (nbg1) and Falkenstein (fsn1) in Germany and Helsinki (hel1) in Finland are all in the eu-central network zone, with similar latency to most of Europe. The type is often in stock at one of the others.
  2. Wait and retry. Capacity comes and goes during the day. My CX23 in Helsinki came back later.
  3. Pick the next family up (CPX), if you can't wait and the price is acceptable.

A consequence I didn't expect: once you hold a scarce server type, deleting the
server to fix a mistake is risky. You may not get another one. That shaped
part 2, where I fixed a setup mistake on the running server instead of
recreating it.

Location and image
  • Location: as close as possible to your users and to your object storage. My storage is a global-anycast S3 provider, so any EU location was fine.
  • Image: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. "LTS" means five years of security updates, which is what you want on a server you'd rather not rebuild. 24.04 LTS would have been equally good.
2. SSH keys: how you'll get in What a key pair is

An SSH key pair is two halves of one mathematical object:

  • the private key (~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519) stays on your laptop and never leaves it;
  • the public key (~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub) goes on every server you want to log in to, in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

The server never learns your private key. At login it asks your SSH client to
sign a value that is unique to this connection. Your client signs it with the
private key, and the server checks the signature against the public key it has
on file. A valid signature proves you hold the private key without the key ever
crossing the network.

Notice there are two key pairs in play:

Key Belongs to Proves Stored where host key the server "I really am 198.51.100.20, not an impostor" server: /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*; your laptop remembers it in ~/.ssh/known_hosts user key you "I'm allowed to log in as ubuntu" laptop: private key; server: authorized_keys

The first time you connect, SSH shows the host key's fingerprint and asks
whether to trust it. This is called TOFU: trust on first use. If the host key
later changes, for example because you rebuilt the server, SSH refuses to connect
and warns about a possible man-in-the-middle. That's correct behaviour. After a
deliberate rebuild, remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R .

Creating the key 
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -C hetzner-api
  • -t ed25519: a modern elliptic-curve key. It's short (one line), fast, and has no weak-parameter choices to get wrong, unlike older RSA keys.
  • -f: the file name. A separate key per provider means losing or rotating one doesn't touch the others.
  • -C: a comment, just a label so you can recognise the key in authorized_keys later.

It asks for a passphrase. Use one: it encrypts the private key on disk, and
ssh-agent remembers it for your session, so you type it once.

Print the public half and paste it into Hetzner → Security → SSH keys → Add
SSH key:

cat ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub

When you pick this key on the create screen, Hetzner writes it into the new
server's /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, and, as a side effect, does not set a
root password at all. Remember that; it matters in part 2.

3. Primary IPs: an address that outlives the server What a Primary IP is

In Hetzner Cloud, a server's public address is a separate resource called a
Primary IP. It's created along with the server and attached to it, but it has
a life of its own:

  • IPv4: one address, billed separately (about $0.60/month), because the world has run out of IPv4.
  • IPv6: a whole /64 network, free. That's 2⁶⁴ addresses; the server uses the first one by convention (2001:db8:1234:5678::1).
Why "auto delete" matters

Each Primary IP has an auto delete switch. On, the address is released when
the server is deleted, and you'll probably never get it back. Off, the address
stays in your project, unattached, ready to assign to a replacement server.

Why you want it off for production:

  • DNS points at it. A new address means a DNS change, and DNS changes take a while to reach everyone (part 3 explains TTLs).
  • Other services may allowlist it. Object-storage tokens, database firewalls and payment-provider webhook settings sometimes filter by source IP.
  • It's your escape hatch. If the server breaks beyond repair, you can delete it and create a new one with the same address.

Turn it off in IPs → (the IPv4) → ⋯. If the menu offers "Enable Auto
Delete", it's already off.

I didn't add an IPv6 (AAAA) DNS record. The old server had none, so the
migration changes as little as possible. That can come later.

4. The Cloud Firewall: the perimeter outside your VM Two places a firewall can sit

A Hetzner Cloud Firewall filters traffic in Hetzner's network, before it
reaches your VM. A host firewall like ufw filters it inside the VM.

The difference matters because of Docker. When a container publishes a port
(ports: ["443:443"]), Docker writes its own NAT rules that send the packet to
the container before it reaches the chain ufw controls. So ufw deny 443
does not block a published Docker port, and plenty of people have exposed a
database to the internet this way while ufw status said everything was closed.

The Cloud Firewall can't be bypassed from inside the VM, so it is the real
perimeter. ufw (set up in part 2) is a second layer for anything that isn't
Docker.

Stateful filtering, in one paragraph

Both firewalls are stateful: they track connections. You write rules for
new incoming connections only. Replies to connections your server opened (to
download packages, call an API, fetch a certificate) are recognised as part of
an existing connection and let back in automatically. That's why the rule set
below has no outbound rules at all: with no outbound rules, Hetzner allows all
outbound traffic, and the server needs outbound access to apt, the container
registry, object storage, the email provider and Let's Encrypt.

The rules

Create it before the server (Firewalls → Create Firewall) so the server is
born protected:

Protocol Port Source Why TCP 2222 Any IPv4, Any IPv6 SSH, on a non-standard port TCP 22 Any SSH, for networks that block outbound 2222 TCP 80 Any Let's Encrypt's HTTP-01 challenge, and the HTTP→HTTPS redirect TCP 443 Any the API UDP 443 Any HTTP/3 (QUIC runs over UDP) ICMP — Any ping, and path-MTU discovery (blocking all ICMP can silently break large packets)

Not on the list: 5432 (Postgres) and 6379 (Valkey). They're never published, and
if a misconfiguration ever did publish them, this firewall would still drop the
traffic.

Why two SSH ports? Port 22 gets a constant stream of automated password-guessing
bots. Moving SSH to 2222 isn't security, since a port scan finds it in seconds,
but it cuts that noise to almost nothing and keeps the logs readable. Key-only
login (part 2) is the actual security. I kept 22 as well, because some networks
block outbound connections to unusual ports. As part 2 shows, my home network
turned out to do the reverse.

5. cloud-init: configuring the server before you first log in What it is

cloud-init is a program in every major cloud image that runs once, on first
boot. It reads "user data" the provider hands to the VM, which is the text you
paste into the Cloud config box on the create screen, and applies it:
creating users, writing files, installing packages, running commands.

The appeal is that the server is configured before anyone logs in. You never
have a window where it's reachable with default settings, and the configuration
is a document you can review and reuse.

#cloud-config
users:
  - name: ubuntu
    groups: [sudo]
    shell: /bin/bash
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - ssh-ed25519 AAAA...your-public-key... hetzner-api
disable_root: true
ssh_pwauth: false
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true
packages: [ufw, unattended-upgrades]
write_files:
  - path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf
    content: |
      Port 22
      Port 2222
      PasswordAuthentication no
      KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
      PermitRootLogin no
      PubkeyAuthentication yes
  - path: /etc/docker/daemon.json
    content: |
      {"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}
runcmd:
  - ufw default deny incoming
  - ufw default allow outgoing
  - ufw allow 22/tcp
  - ufw allow 2222/tcp
  - ufw allow 80/tcp
  - ufw allow 443/tcp
  - ufw allow 443/udp
  - ufw --force enable
  - systemctl daemon-reload
  - systemctl restart ssh.socket || true
  - systemctl restart ssh || true
  - fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile
  - echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' >> /etc/fstab

Every line here is explained in part 2, where we apply the same settings by hand.

The order cloud-init works in

One thing that will surprise you if you SSH in too early: cloud-init runs its
stages in order, and package_upgrade comes before runcmd. On a fresh image
the upgrade can take a few minutes, and during that time port 2222 isn't open yet.
cloud-init status --wait blocks until everything has finished.

What actually happened

I created the server with the type, location, image, SSH key and firewall all
set, and forgot to paste the cloud config. The box came up as a stock image:
only root, only port 22, no ubuntu user, no ufw, no swap. My first
ssh -p 2222 got Connection refused.

"Refused" is useful information. It means the packet reached the machine (the
Cloud Firewall allowed it) and the kernel answered "nothing is listening here".
A firewall drop would have shown up as a timeout instead. Part 2 goes into
that difference.

Since CX23 was close to sold out, I didn't delete and recreate. I applied the same
configuration by hand, as root over port 22. That's part 2.

6. Create

The final create screen, for reference:

Field Value Location Helsinki (or wherever the type is in stock) Image Ubuntu 26.04 LTS Type Shared vCPU → Cost-Optimized → x86 → CX23 Networking Public IPv4 ✅, Public IPv6 ✅ SSH keys hetzner-api Firewalls the firewall from section 4 Backups off (the database is backed up to object storage; see part 3) Cloud config the YAML above. Don't forget it Name something meaningful. The default ubuntu-4gb-hel1-1 tells you nothing in six months

Then turn off auto delete on the new IPv4 (section 3), and check that the
firewall shows "Fully applied" with one server.

What we have so far
  • a CX23 with 4 GB RAM for about $7/month including IPv4;
  • an IPv4 address that survives the server;
  • a perimeter firewall that allows only SSH, HTTP(S) and ICMP;
  • a stock Ubuntu, reachable as root on port 22 only, because the cloud config was never applied.

In part 2 we fix that by hand: a non-root user, key-only SSH on two ports,
ufw, swap, automatic security updates and Docker. Along the way: how to configure
two servers in ~/.ssh/config, how to make changes over SSH without locking
yourself out, and how to tell from a port test whether a firewall or a closed
port is in your way.

items.title: Edge0 Releases Audio8-TTS-Realistic, a 0.6B Voice Cloning TTS Model
items.summary:
Edge0 has released Audio8-TTS-Realistic , an open-weight text-to-speech model for zero-shot voice cloning. Audio8-TTS-Realistic is a 0.6B-parameter model that clones a voice from 1 reference clip and transcript. It supports 23 languages, 12 more than its predecessor. The weights and code ship under Apache 2.0 . For developers, the catch is competitive multilingual accuracy at a size that is cheap to fine-tune and serve. TL;DR Size: 601M main-model parameters (codec excluded); up to 2,048 packed text/audio positions of context. Runs on: a CUDA GPU is recommended; smoke-tested on NVIDIA H20 in BF16. The paper reports 1.1 to 1.2 GiB peak memory on an Apple M2 CPU (INT4 ONNX). No Realistic ONNX export is public yet. Performance: ahead of larger open models on CV3, behind 4B-class models on MiniMax. Best: 4.86% average CV3 error across 9 languages, versus 7.73% for Qwen3-TTS-1.7B. Worst: 48.57% WER on Thai (CV3) and 31.35% CER on Cantonese (MiniMax). What is Audio8-TTS-Realistic? It is the second 0.6B release in Edge0’s Audio8 TTS family. It builds on Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b and keeps the same Transformers inference interface. The repository bundles the checkpoint, a 44.1 kHz neural audio codec, tokenizer, processor and custom code. It can also generate speech without a reference voice. New languages are Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish and Vietnamese. How does the architecture work? The model uses a dual-autoregressive (DualAR) design inspired by Fish Audio S2 Pro . According to the technical research report , the slow branch is built on Qwen2.5 0.5B. It has 24 layers at width 896 and runs at about 21.5 frames per second. Each step predicts text tokens plus the first audio codebook. A shallow 4-layer fast branch then predicts the remaining 9 codebooks in parallel. Sequential compute therefore happens only at the frame level. How does Edge0 train for realism? The team argues that word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) miss rhythm, pauses and timing. A model can score well on both and still sound synthetic. Training runs in 3 stages: Multilingual supervised fine-tuning (SFT). GRPO with a combined reward: 0.7 weight on WER, 0.3 on SIM. GRPO guided by a learned realism critic. The critic scores each output against a matched human recording of the same sentence. It was trained on a quality ladder built from 6 open-source TTS systems. These were ranked in a private blind listening study, with human recordings at the top. Synthetic pause compression adds finer rungs to the ladder. An identity-erasure loss stops the critic from rewarding generator fingerprints. The critic head has about 3M parameters on top of a frozen WavLM-large encoder. A duration penalty also kicks in beyond 1.35x the reference length. This blocks the policy from gaming the critic with slower speech. The final stage used only Chinese and English prompts. It still improved both aggregate metrics on the 13 lower-resource languages. Their error fell from 22.53% to 20.77%, and SIM rose from 0.637 to 0.679.

Edge0 · Open-weight TTS · Apache 2.0

Audio8-TTS-Realistic, explained

Zero-shot voice cloning in 601M parameters, trained with a learned realism critic.

STAGE 2GRPO: WER + SIMReward weights 0.7 on WER, 0.3 on speaker similarity.
STAGE 3GRPO: realism criticScores each output against a matched human recording.

The realism stage used only Chinese and English prompts, yet improved both metrics on the 13 additional languages. Source: technical report, Table 1.

CV3 error rate per language (CER for Chinese, Japanese, Korean; WER otherwise). 500 items each. Shorter bar is better.

Transformers (PyTorch 2.5+, Transformers 4.57+, CUDA GPU recommended):

model_id = "Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)

Serving: SGLang Omni adapter with paged attention, dynamic batching and an OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API. Throughput and streaming were not benchmarked by Edge0.

CPU: the paper reports 1.1 to 1.2 GiB peak on an Apple M2 with INT4 ONNX. The repo states no Realistic ONNX export is available yet.

Numbers self-reported by Edge0; competitor figures from their own sources or Boson AI's evaluation.© Marktechpost
"> How does it perform on benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported error rates, where lower is better. Seed-TTS (English/Chinese): 1.25% average error, SIM 0.704. CV3 (9 languages): 4.86% average error, SIM 0.661. MiniMax (24 languages): 5.89% average error, SIM 0.754. On CV3, Audio8 beats VoxCPM2 (5.35%), CosyVoice3-1.5B (6.89%) and Qwen3-TTS-1.7B (7.73%). On MiniMax, Qwen3-TTS-1.7B scores 27.41%, but it officially supports only 10 of the 24 test languages. Larger models still lead elsewhere. Higgs TTS 3 reports 4.41% on CV3 and 2.74% on MiniMax. Qwen3-TTS-1.7B averages 1.01% on Seed-TTS. Edge0 itself calls its table a reference comparison, since evaluation pipelines and text normalization differ. How does it compare with other open TTS models? Feature Audio8-TTS-Realistic Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base VoxCPM2 Higgs TTS 3 Size 0.6B (excl. codec) 1.7B 2B ~4B backbone License Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Research and non-commercial Languages 23 10 30 100+ Output sample rate 44.1 kHz Not disclosed 48 kHz 24 kHz Seed-TTS EN WER 1.46% 1.24% 1.84% Not disclosed Seed-TTS ZH CER 1.03% 0.77% 0.97% Not disclosed CV3 avg error (9 langs) 4.86% 7.73% (Boson AI eval) 5.35% 4.41% MiniMax avg error (24 langs) 5.89% 27.41% (Boson AI eval) Not disclosed 2.74% Hardware noted CUDA GPU; INT4 M2 CPU in paper GPU, FlashAttention 2 ~8 GB VRAM 1x H100 serving tests VoxCPM2’s CV3 average is computed from its per-language table. How do you deploy it? Install PyTorch 2.5+ and Transformers 4.57+, then load with trust_remote_code=True . Voice cloning needs a clean reference clip and its exact transcript. The GitHub repo adds a CLI, batching and supervised fine-tuning scripts. For GPU serving, an SGLang Omni adapter provides paged attention, dynamic batching and an OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API. Edge0 notes throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. A free Playground runs on Hugging Face ZeroGPU. Key Takeaways 601M parameters, 23 languages, Apache 2.0 weights. A learned realism critic drives the final GRPO stage. 4.86% CV3 error beats Qwen3-TTS-1.7B and VoxCPM2. 4B-class Higgs TTS 3 still leads on CV3 and MiniMax. Lower-resource languages remain weak, with Thai near 49% WER. Check out the Paper , Model Weights , Repo and Samples . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Edge0 has released Audio8-TTS-Realistic, an open-weight text-to-speech model for zero-shot voice cloning. Audio8-TTS-Realistic is a 0.6B-parameter model that clones a voice from 1 reference clip and transcript. It supports 23 languages, 12 more than its predecessor. The weights and code ship under Apache 2.0. For developers, the catch is competitive multilingual accuracy at a size that is cheap to fine-tune and serve.

TL;DR
  • Size: 601M main-model parameters (codec excluded); up to 2,048 packed text/audio positions of context.
  • Runs on: a CUDA GPU is recommended; smoke-tested on NVIDIA H20 in BF16. The paper reports 1.1 to 1.2 GiB peak memory on an Apple M2 CPU (INT4 ONNX). No Realistic ONNX export is public yet.
  • Performance: ahead of larger open models on CV3, behind 4B-class models on MiniMax.
  • Best: 4.86% average CV3 error across 9 languages, versus 7.73% for Qwen3-TTS-1.7B.
  • Worst: 48.57% WER on Thai (CV3) and 31.35% CER on Cantonese (MiniMax).
What is Audio8-TTS-Realistic?

It is the second 0.6B release in Edge0’s Audio8 TTS family. It builds on Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b and keeps the same Transformers inference interface. The repository bundles the checkpoint, a 44.1 kHz neural audio codec, tokenizer, processor and custom code. It can also generate speech without a reference voice.

New languages are Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish and Vietnamese.

How does the architecture work?

The model uses a dual-autoregressive (DualAR) design inspired by Fish Audio S2 Pro. According to the technical research report, the slow branch is built on Qwen2.5 0.5B. It has 24 layers at width 896 and runs at about 21.5 frames per second. Each step predicts text tokens plus the first audio codebook.

A shallow 4-layer fast branch then predicts the remaining 9 codebooks in parallel. Sequential compute therefore happens only at the frame level.

How does Edge0 train for realism?

The team argues that word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) miss rhythm, pauses and timing. A model can score well on both and still sound synthetic.

Training runs in 3 stages:

  1. Multilingual supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
  2. GRPO with a combined reward: 0.7 weight on WER, 0.3 on SIM.
  3. GRPO guided by a learned realism critic.

The critic scores each output against a matched human recording of the same sentence. It was trained on a quality ladder built from 6 open-source TTS systems. These were ranked in a private blind listening study, with human recordings at the top. Synthetic pause compression adds finer rungs to the ladder.

An identity-erasure loss stops the critic from rewarding generator fingerprints. The critic head has about 3M parameters on top of a frozen WavLM-large encoder. A duration penalty also kicks in beyond 1.35x the reference length. This blocks the policy from gaming the critic with slower speech.

The final stage used only Chinese and English prompts. It still improved both aggregate metrics on the 13 lower-resource languages. Their error fell from 22.53% to 20.77%, and SIM rose from 0.637 to 0.679.

How does it perform on benchmarks?

All numbers below are self-reported error rates, where lower is better.

  • Seed-TTS (English/Chinese): 1.25% average error, SIM 0.704.
  • CV3 (9 languages): 4.86% average error, SIM 0.661.
  • MiniMax (24 languages): 5.89% average error, SIM 0.754.

On CV3, Audio8 beats VoxCPM2 (5.35%), CosyVoice3-1.5B (6.89%) and Qwen3-TTS-1.7B (7.73%). On MiniMax, Qwen3-TTS-1.7B scores 27.41%, but it officially supports only 10 of the 24 test languages.

Larger models still lead elsewhere. Higgs TTS 3 reports 4.41% on CV3 and 2.74% on MiniMax. Qwen3-TTS-1.7B averages 1.01% on Seed-TTS. Edge0 itself calls its table a reference comparison, since evaluation pipelines and text normalization differ.

How do you deploy it?

Install PyTorch 2.5+ and Transformers 4.57+, then load with trust_remote_code=True. Voice cloning needs a clean reference clip and its exact transcript. The GitHub repo adds a CLI, batching and supervised fine-tuning scripts.

For GPU serving, an SGLang Omni adapter provides paged attention, dynamic batching and an OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API. Edge0 notes throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. A free Playground runs on Hugging Face ZeroGPU.

Key Takeaways
  • 601M parameters, 23 languages, Apache 2.0 weights.
  • A learned realism critic drives the final GRPO stage.
  • 4.86% CV3 error beats Qwen3-TTS-1.7B and VoxCPM2.
  • 4B-class Higgs TTS 3 still leads on CV3 and MiniMax.
  • Lower-resource languages remain weak, with Thai near 49% WER.

items.title: OpenAI Doubles ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium Usage Limits After Dropping a Planned Pro 200 Cut
items.summary: OpenAI has doubled usage limits for its $100, $200, and $500 ChatGPT Pro plans and for Business Premium, effective October 29. The announcement came from Tibo, who represents ChatGPT and Codex on X, and it replaces an earlier plan to reduce the usage allowance for existing Pro 200 subscribers after October 29. "We are doubling all usage limits for all Pro 100/200/500 tiers and Business Premium, effective today," Tibo wrote. The company says it reversed course following customer feedback. OpenAI Reverses the Planned ChatGPT Pro 200 Usage Cut OpenAI had planned to lower the included usage allowance for Pro 200 subscribers while keeping the subscription price at $200 per month. That cut is now off the table. "We heard your kind feedback and won't be reducing usage limits for Pro 200, so your Work and Codex usage will stay the same," Tibo said in the same post. The higher limits mainly affect ChatGPT Work and Codex, which share usage allowances under eligible subscriptions. Pro subscribers who rely on Codex for coding tasks or on Work for longer jobs get more room before they hit the cap, without moving to a more expensive tier. OpenAI is also keeping extended limits for Dots, its always-on AI assistants. "We're also going to continue offering extended limits for Dots for now, and usage of your dot will still continue to be separate from your default usage," the company said. Dots usage therefore does not draw from the doubled Work and Codex allowance. The change follows a busy month for OpenAI pricing, including the launch of GPT-6.1 Terra with lower API pricing earlier this week. What ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium Subscribers Should Check No action is required to receive the higher limits, since OpenAI applied them to eligible accounts immediately. Subscribers can still use the change to review their plans: Pro 200 subscribers who were preparing to switch plans because of the announced cut keep their previous Work and Codex usage, now doubled. Pro 100 subscribers who regularly reach their cap get twice the allowance at the same $100 price. Pro 500 and Business Premium customers receive the same doubling on their existing allowance. Dots users keep a separate allowance that does not count against default usage. OpenAI does not publish exact numerical usage limits for each tier, so subscribers cannot verify the doubling against a published figure. The company also describes the extended Dots limits as available "for now" and has not said how long they will stay in place. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: Behind DeepSeek’s $16 Billion Funding: Chinese Tech Titans and State Players
items.summary: Chinese AI star DeepSeek’s nearly $16 billion funding round this month involved not only a deluge of capital but a who’s who of Chinese tech investors—and some of the country’s most powerful state-backed institutions, according to details of the round obtained by The Information. It was only the second fundraising round for DeepSeek. The three-year-old company was the only major AI model developer to eschew external capital until its first fundraising in April. The new round included previous backers—Tencent and battery maker CATL continue to be DeepSeek’s top two investors—but also other tech companies including notably memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies and its chairman Zhu Yiming, according to the details provided by two people with direct knowledge of the matter.

items.title: DoorDash and Thrive Go Shopping
items.summary: Get your deals in while ya still can, folks. And clearly, there are relative bargains to be had. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu gets what I’m talking about. On Thursday, Xu finally picked up Instacart, with Xu’s company saying it would pay about $17 billion for the grocery-delivery business. Over on X, Instacart founder Apoorva Mehta sent up a resounding huzzah , saying he and Xu had long discussed such a transaction. That wasn’t news to readers of The Information: We reported on talks between DoorDash and Instacart back in 2021. At one point in 2021, DoorDash was considering buying Instacart for more than $40 billion. By waiting, Xu obviously saved himself a bunch of money and avoided the ridiculous markups that were attached to pandemic-era darlings like Instacart. Sure, its prospects seemed rosier back then, when we were regarding physical grocery stores as potentially lethal germ pools, but Xu doesn’t seem to be getting a total lemon. In the third quarter, Instacart sales grew 17%, and it generated a decent amount of cash in that time—more than $300 million, a 13% increase. The sale to Xu does solve Instacart’s leadership problem: It had looked rather rudderless since Fidji Simo left the CEO role for OpenAI in 2025. Still, Xu will need to figure out how to handle the fierce competition for online grocery sales, a battle that includes Walmart and Amazon (more on the latter company below). One thing that held Xu up in 2021 was concern about the Biden administration. According to Valida’s reporting, Xu figured DoorDash wouldn’t get an Instacart acquisition past Biden regulators, who, of course, were trying their hardest to squelch corporate mergers and acquisitions. Those days of dealmaking famine have given way to a time of great feasting: The Trump White House has been, uh, lenient with regulatory approval. It could all shift once again after the midterms. With Democrats seemingly set to retake Congress next week, and President Donald Trump enjoying the same popularity as a DoorDasher who shows up with a carton of broken eggs, the idea of a liberal in the White House after 2028 seems a lot more plausible than it did even a few months ago. The prospect of a Democrat in the White House will spur plenty more M&A to happen sooner rather than later. I get it. Judging by the words of liberal standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, the left’s attitude toward mergers does not seem to have changed much since President Joe Biden creaked out of office. On Thursday, Mamdani criticized the DoorDash-Instacart deal, saying in a post on X that such moves often bring higher prices for consumers and “harsher exploitation” for workers. In addition to politics, M&A sure seems likely to keep humming for the simple reason that there are plenty of other Instacarts out there—businesses that haven’t fared well since their pandemic glory days. Zoom, Duolingo, Coursera: I could go on. I would’ve put Bumble right there, too, had it not already limped into the welcoming arms of investor Ravi Gupta several weeks ago. (Gupta bought Bumble for about $6 a share; Bumble once traded hands at more than $75.) Other M&A action seems like it’ll be driven by the chance to spruce up an aging business with AI, which I imagine is the motivating force behind the other deal announced on Thursday: Josh Kushner’s $7.6 billion purchase of ADT, maker of home security systems, through the newly formed Thrive Holdings, an offshoot of his Thrive Capital. Another reason that I’m going on and on about M&A today is because I listened to what Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett, the bank’s global co-head of investment banking, had to say about the topic at our WTF conference earlier this week. By the sounds of things, her direct messages are cluttered with missives from deal-hungry CEOs. “They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape. CEOs are leaning in right now—they wanna make big strategic bets,” she said. “We’re optimistic.” Still, as she pointed out, “things change quickly.” —Abram Brown Amazon’s Agita If there’s a lesson in the earnings reports from Amazon and Google over the past couple of days, it’s that investors are more in the mood to focus on the companies’ blemishes rather than the strong performance of their cloud units. On Thursday, Amazon said revenues from its Amazon Web Services unit had surged 39% to $45.98 billion, its strongest growth rate in nearly four years. That was an impressive feat given that second-quarter AWS revenues grew at a record 37%. And if that wasn’t enough, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy forecast AWS growth rates of over 40% in 2027 and 2028. On a call with analysts, Jassy went even further and predicted that AWS could be one of two businesses for Amazon with $1 trillion a year revenue within the next five to 10 years (the other is its stores business—Amazon-speak for its e-commerce business and everything else, excluding AWS). But, it turns out, that was not enough for investors, many of whom are increasingly on edge about whether tech giants will see a sustainable payoff from the colossal amounts of money they’re spending on AI. Amazon shares dropped more than 6% in after-hours trading. The company’s total net sales were $201.9 billion, up 12%, while its net income was $20.7 billion, down slightly from a year earlier, when it had a pre-tax gain of $9.5 billion from its investment in Anthropic. Even though Amazon’s numbers were within its own forecasts, Wall Street analysts were expecting slightly better results. The company left its estimate for its 2026 capital expenditures—most of which is going to its spending on data centers—unchanged at $220 billion. Google had a similar experience today. Investors punished its stock, sending it down 12%. It appears they were more keen to focus on the bad in its Wednesday earnings report (sluggish revenue growth in its core search advertising business) rather than the good (a doubling of Google Cloud revenues). The AI glass seems to be half full for many investors right now. —Nick Wingfield In Other News U.S. intelligence agencies found that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese spy. Over on X, Instacart founder Apoorva Mehta sent up a resounding huzzah, saying he and Xu had long discussed such a transaction. According to Valida’s reporting, Xu figured DoorDash wouldn’t get an Instacart acquisition past Biden regulators, who, of course, were trying their hardest to squelch corporate mergers and acquisitions. Those days of dealmaking famine have given way to a time of great feasting: The Trump White House has been, uh, lenient with regulatory approval. It could all shift once again after the midterms. With Democrats seemingly set to retake Congress next week, and President Donald Trump enjoying the same popularity as a DoorDasher who shows up with a carton of broken eggs, the idea of a liberal in the White House after 2028 seems a lot more plausible than it did even a few months ago. 

The prospect of a Democrat in the White House will spur plenty more M&A to happen sooner rather than later. I get it. Judging by the words of liberal standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, the left’s attitude toward mergers does not seem to have changed much since President Joe Biden creaked out of office. On Thursday, Mamdani criticized the DoorDash-Instacart deal, saying in a post on X that such moves often bring higher prices for consumers and “harsher exploitation” for workers.

Zoom, Duolingo, Coursera: I could go on. I would’ve put Bumble right there, too, had it not already limped into the welcoming arms of investor Ravi Gupta several weeks ago. (Gupta bought Bumble for about $6 a share; Bumble once traded hands at more than $75.) By the sounds of things, her direct messages are cluttered with missives from deal-hungry CEOs.

“They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape. CEOs are leaning in right now—they wanna make big strategic bets,” she said. “We’re optimistic.” Still, as she pointed out, “things change quickly.”—Abram Brown

Amazon’s Agita

If there’s a lesson in the earnings reports from Amazon and Google over the past couple of days, it’s that investors are more in the mood to focus on the companies’ blemishes rather than the strong performance of their cloud units. 

On Thursday, Amazon said revenues from its Amazon Web Services unit had surged 39% to $45.98 billion, its strongest growth rate in nearly four years. That was an impressive feat given that second-quarter AWS revenues grew at a record 37%. And if that wasn’t enough, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy forecast AWS growth rates of over 40% in 2027 and 2028. 

On a call with analysts, Jassy went even further and predicted that AWS could be one of two businesses for Amazon with $1 trillion a year revenue within the next five to 10 years (the other is its stores business—Amazon-speak for its e-commerce business and everything else, excluding AWS).
